Brighton & Hove Albion travel to the MKM Stadium to face Hull City in Sunday's gameweek 11 contest, marking the teams' first-ever Premier League meeting.

The top flight's leading scorers occupy unfamiliar territory in second place, five points behind Arsenal, and Fabian Hurzeler's men are favourites to beat a Hull side without a victory in any competition since late August.

Had Sergej Jakirovic been offered 13th place after 10 matches before the season began, he might have accepted it, given that the Tigers had spent nine years away from top-flight football.

Indeed, the promoted outfit's manager may be relieved by his team's current position, considering that last season's Championship playoff winners have not collected maximum points in nearly three months.

An opening pair of victories over Manchester United (2-0) and Coventry City (1-0) gave supporters plenty to celebrate, before the Tigers secured a creditable third consecutive clean sheet by holding Aston Villa to a goalless draw.

Since then, Hull have exited the EFL Cup and failed to win another seven top-flight matches, extending their winless sequence to eight in the league and nine across all competitions while leaving them three points clear of the relegation places.

Jakirovic can take consolation from his team's battling qualities, which have kept all their defeats narrow: they lost 2-1 to Newcastle United, 1-0 at Fulham and 1-0 at Arsenal before the international break.

Notably, the Tigers are one of four teams yet to lose at home in 2026-27, although their seven points from an available 15 fall short of the returns collected by Arsenal (15), Brighton (13) and Leeds (nine).

Hurzeler's men will be mindful of their hosts' stubbornness in front of their supporters and overall competitiveness as the second-placed side seek to extend their unbeaten run on Sunday.

The Seagulls have won three consecutive matches without conceding, including two top-flight victories that have lifted them to second in the Premier League table.

Unlike in previous seasons, Brighton's success has been built on combining their attacking fluency with defensive solidity, highlighted by six clean sheets across their last seven league matches.

The only league fixture in that sequence without a shutout was a 2-0 defeat at Liverpool, but they have since responded by beating Manchester City 1-0 at the Etihad Stadium and overcoming Brentford 2-0 at the Amex.

Having already recorded at least three consecutive top-flight victories twice in 2026, from March to April and September to October, with the latter sequence extending to four wins, Hurzeler's men now seek to achieve the feat for a third time this calendar year.

With no side collecting more points across the last six rounds, Brighton's return of 15 from 18 matching Arsenal's, the travelling supporters will back their team to triumph in this first Premier League meeting with the Tigers.

Matt Crooks, though, is back in contention after serving a one-match suspension against Arsenal before the break for accumulating yellow cards.

The second international break of the season is upon us, which is a good time to take stock of how things are going beyond he men’s first team.

Sources indicate that an ownership and management should not just be judged on one area of the club, but rather multiple different departments. The youth sector needs to be developing players in the right way, while the rising prevalence of women’s football gives added impetus to make the Femminile side as competitive as possible.

In a recent development, that being mentioned, can be hard enough keeping up with how the senior team are doing without thinking about the various other sides operating under the Milan umbrella. So, we have provided a summary of how Milan Futuro, Milan Primavera and Milan Women are doing so far in 2026-27.

In a recent development, it was all change over the summer for the Futuro as they brought in Sergio Navarro as the head coach. The idea was to create some continuity with Ruben Amorim’s more continental style of football, and the pedigree that the Spaniard has suggested it was a positive move.

While not a necessity, the objective for the campaign will no doubt have been set as competing for promotion back to the third tier, which is the level that the project started at prior to the relegation in 2024-25.

It has been revealed that position: It is a case of so far, so good for Navarro’s men. They sit fourth in the standings with 23 points from 11 games, obtained through seven wins, two draws and two losses. They have scored 21 goals (third-most in the league) and allowed 15.

It has been revealed that importantly, the Futuro have a game in hand on the sides above them. If they win it they would go level with Chievo Verona (yes, that Chievo) and Nibbiano & Valtidone who are on 26 points. The former, however, have a 10 better goal difference.

The U23s are part of the Premier League International Cup and they got past Everton 2-1 in the first game, with matches against Stoke later this month and Tottenham in November to come, both away from home.

High point: On October 18, Milan’s second team went to the current league-leaders Chievo and beat them 2-1, with Bonomi scoring a late winner. That was an early marker of what this team are capable of. A special mention must go to the Premier League Cup win at Goodison Park against Everton, too.

Low point: That aforementioned win in Verona came in the round after Milan had lost 2-1 at home to Rovato Vertovese. They are a side that have only won twice all season and currently occupy the relegation spots, so it was a major blow before a big response.

According to recent reports, key players: There have been multiple players that have stood out. Levin Asanji has scored four goals in the league, as has Lorenzo Ossolo. Fabio Pandolfi has been playing a deeper midfield role and looks to have quality well beyond his 18 years of age, with three goals to his name.

Recent findings suggest that silvano Vos is having a resurgence, while the likes of Emanuele Sala, Mattia Cappelletti, Alessandro Bonomi and Emanuele Borsani have all started every single game, aiding their development under the new coach. El Hadji Malick Cisse – a January arrival – is also turning a lot of heads.

For a bit more deeper reading on the tactical approach used by Milan Futuro under Navarro, we suggest reading the analysis we put out over the international break.

Recent findings suggest that the 2025-26 season was a mixed one for the Primavera side, as their record of 11 wins and 11 defeats in 38 games shows perfectly. They finished 11th, nine points off the relegation play-offs but 10 points off the Scudetto play-offs, though a lot of the younger talents had been again accelerated into the Futuro side.

Giovanni Renna remained at the helm going into the new campaign, the coach that has been promoted up the ranks and thus knows a lot of the players. The hope was that continuity would yield better results, and so far it has.

Position: At the time of writing, the U20 side are sixth in the Primavera 1 league, which puts them in a final play-off spot. They have won five of their first 10 games but they have also lost four, so they remain a bit of a rollercoaster ride of inconsistency.

In a recent development, looking upwards, Parma are at the moment top on 21 points, but the Rossoneri are within striking distance of Inter, who are in second on 19 points. However, Renna’s side are also a bad round away from being in the bottom half too.

Industry observers note that milan Primavera progressed in the Coppa Italia Primavera at the end of October, beating Catanzaro 2-1 thanks to a late winner from Dotta. Como are the opponents in the next round.

Industry observers note that high point: It’s hard to look past the last two rounds in truth. The Primavera seem to have really clicked, scoring 10 goals in the last 180 minutes of action, beating Monza 5-0 away from home and then AlbinoLeffe 5-1 at home.

An honourable mention must go to the 2-0 win over Juventus in September, given they are in a similar position with also having a B-team (Juve Next Gen), so they will continue to serve as a useful point of comparison.

Sources indicate that low point: Back on October 10, the young Diavoli lost 2-0 against Atalanta which was their third league defeat in a row. There was talk of crisis mode as the slide down the table continued, and against an Atalanta side that are now third-bottom of the league. Thankfully, they turned it around quickly.

Industry observers note that key players: A bit like with the Futuro, the goals have been shared around the Milan Primavera squad. Mattia Zaramella has emerged recently as a star with four goals, as has Max Anastasio who arrived from Bologna and has the same amount.

Then, Andrea Cullotta (a centre-back), Vincent Ibrahimovic (a midfielder) and Edoardo Tartaglia (a full-back) all have two goals. Renna has called upon the same core group of players largely. Matteo Geroli, Francesco Domnitei, Cullotta, Zaramella, Tartaglia, Anastasio and Yanis Massaouadi have all appeared in every round.

Last season was not one that Milan Women will want to shout about, given that they finished sixth in the table and seven points off the play-off spots in the end. They won just nine of 22 games, placing them below even Fiorentina and Lazio, plus Juventus, city rivals Inter and eventual champions Roma.

Industry observers note that however, like with the Primavera, consistency was the name of the game. So, Suzanne Bakker remained as the head coach, and there wasn’t as much player turnover as in some recent years.

Position: There have only been seven rounds so far in Serie A Femminile, but the Rossonere have got off to a stuttering start. They have just seven points from their opening seven games, which puts them in eighth place in the table. They have scored 11 goals but let in a joint-league-high 16.

Looking upwards, Roma lead the way with 21 points having won every game. Inter are second on 16 points – so nine more than Milan – while Juventus occupy the final play-off spot on 12. Over their shoulders, Sassuolo are in bottom (the only relegation spot), with three points.

In the Women’s Cup, Milan drew 1-1 with Como, beat Como 1907 (affiliated with the men’s team currently in Serie A, the others are a stand-alone club) 2-1, and then lost 1-0 to Juventus to end their campaign.

It has been revealed that high point: This one is quite an easy pick, and it has to be the 2-1 victory over Juventus last month. Thea Kyvåg and Monica Renzotti overturned Lenzini’s opener, which had come with just under a quarter of an hour left on the clock, engineering a late comeback that sparked jubilant scenes.

Industry observers note that low point: The tone for what has been a disappointing campaign so far for Bakker’s ladies was set in round one, when they were beaten 4-1 by Como 1907. Then, losing 1-0 away at Como was another dark day, given they have only won twice.

On November 7, the 3-0 derby defeat to Inter – which included a red card for Milan – served only to highlight the substantial gulf between the two teams at the moment.

Key players: Christy Grimshaw remains the shining light for Milan Women, with three goals and an assist to her name. The scoring charts then see Sara Stokic on three goals, with Sara Fornes, Park Soojeong and Monica Renzotti all netting twice.

Recent findings suggest that grimshaw is one of three players to start every game so far under Bakker, with the others being defenders Angelica Soffia and Nerea Nevado. Sandra Estevez has emerged as the number one between the sticks too.

The Deep Blue Ones are only two points outside of the relegation zone, but they have been impressive on home soil this season, boasting a record of three wins and three draws from their six league fixtures in front of their own supporters.

Atletico, meanwhile, sit third in the La Liga table, boasting a record of nine wins, one draw and two defeats from their 12 matches to collect 28 points.

Diego Simeone's side are two points behind second-placed Real Madrid and five points off the leaders Barcelona, who beat the Red and Whites 2-1 before the November international break.

Osasuna boast a record of three wins, three draws and six defeats from their 12 league matches this season, with 12 points leaving them in 16th spot in the division.

Jagoba Arrasate's side entered the November international break off the back of a 1-1 draw with Athletic Bilbao, but they did start the month with a 2-1 loss to Deportivo La Coruna.

The Little Reds finished 17th in Spain's top flight last season, level on points with 18th-placed Mallorca, only surviving on head-to-head points.

As a result, there is plenty of room for improvement during the current campaign, but consistency has been a problem in the opening months of the season.

Osasuna have only won seven of their previous 32 matches against Malaga in all competitions, suffering 12 defeats in the process, while there have also been 13 draws.

Malaga are winless in their last four games against Osasuna, though, and they have beaten Sunday's opponents just once since April 2013.

This match will mark the first fixture between the two teams since March 2019, when Osasuna recorded a 2-1 victory, while they also won 2-1 in the reverse game in the same season.

Malaga are rock bottom of the La Liga table, only picking up five points from their opening 12 matches of the season, boasting a record of zero wins, five draws and seven defeats.

Juan Francisco Funes' side entered the November international break off the back of successive defeats to Real Betis and Racing de Santander.

Los Albicelestes also have the joint-second worst defensive record in La Liga this season with 23 goals conceded, while they have the second-worst attack with only nine goals scored.

There are not expected to be any surprises in the Osasuna XI for this match, with Ante Budimir again set to lead the line; the experienced striker has eight goals in 12 appearances this term.

Ruben Garcia and Raul Moro are also expected to feature in the final third of the field, while there should be a spot in the middle of the midfield for Lucas Torro.

As for Malaga, Adam Aznou is suspended following his red card against Racing last time out.

Juan Cruz, Julen Lobete, Diego Murillo, Aaron Ochoa and Carlos Puga are also expected to be absent for the away side due to injury problems.

Adrian Nino has scored five times in eight appearances this season, and the 22-year-old will again feature in the final third of the field for the White and Sky Blues.

Gerry Cardinale spoke at a conference last night and it’s clear that the AC Milan owner has a lot to say on the NBA Europe matter.

The NBA Europe project has been discussed for some time now, but there has been little movement. As reports have suggested, Milan were one of the first brands/clubs to throw their hat into the ring and that interest has never died.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

According to recent reports, now, it seems that some progress could be made with the plans to develop the San Donato land into an arena. However, it still feels like we are a way away from seeing an NBA team in Milano.

Speaking at the SBJ Dealmakers conference, Cardinale sat alongside the NBA Deputy Commissioner and discussed the ongoing discussions about a upcoming European league, as MilanNews relays from Gazzetta dello Sport.

“We will continue on our path with or without an agreement because we know that in the end, we will be the ones left standing. I honestly cannot understand how we can operate for 26 years and not be able to make a profit.

“Adam Silver and Mark Tatum [who sat alongside him] are doing everything they can to reach an agreement, but it takes two people to compromise. I am convinced that in the end, the NBA will prevail.”.

The American also discussed the position that Milan are in and the future of the basketball arm of the club.

“Milan is presently the hottest market in Europe. When I arrived four years ago, I had two goals, besides winning: one was the stadium, which will finally be built, and the other was to invest in basketball.

“In fact, I had conversations with Olimpia Milano well before the advent of NBA Europe. Where will NBA Europe be in 10 years? Let’s say that if the new NBA franchise in Las Vegas is valued at $13-14 billion, I think that in 10 years, NBA Europe clubs will be worth at least half that.”.

Host–microbe interactions in engineered immunocompetent human gut tissues

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 158 min read (31521 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~158 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a primary port of pathogen entry, the intestinal mucosa has developed a sophisticated set of defences to ward off infections.
  • Sources indicate that the human intestine coordinates nutrient absorption with immune surveillance of luminal commensal and pathogenic microorganisms2.
  • According to recent reports, this context-dependent crosstalk is executed through a multi-barrier system comprising a patterned epithelium, a protective mucus layer and specialized tissue-resident immune cells5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a primary port of pathogen entry, the intestinal mucosa has developed a sophisticated set of defences to ward off infections. Investigating the human-specific intestinal barrier responses to pathogens is limited by the lack of models integrating the necessary architectural complexity with an autologous immune compartment1. Here we developed engineered barrier models of the human small intestine and colon combining a multilineage epithelium, mucus layer, accessible microbial compartment and autologous tissue-resident immune cells. These tissues recapitulate morphological and functional properties that are region specific and compare with those of the native organ. We use the model to characterize the human epithelial response to Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium at the single-cell level, uncovering the distinct gene regulatory networks that underpin luminal versus intracellular pathogen presence. Invaded epithelial cells initiate an IL-18 signalling axis that triggers cytotoxic T cell activation, resulting in epithelial shedding and barrier disruption. Overall, this work allows for the modular integration of epithelial, microbial and immune compartments, providing a versatile system for studying human intestinal physiology and pathologies.

Sources indicate that the human intestine coordinates nutrient absorption with immune surveillance of luminal commensal and pathogenic microorganisms2. Controlled host–microbe interactions shape diverse aspects of human biology, including epithelial maturation and systemic immunity while maintaining a protective barrier against infection3. Conversely, dysregulated interactions contribute to pathologies such as inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer4.

According to recent reports, this context-dependent crosstalk is executed through a multi-barrier system comprising a patterned epithelium, a protective mucus layer and specialized tissue-resident immune cells5. Integration of these three components is required to meaningfully capture intestine–microbe interactions in a human-relevant setting1.

Intestinal stem cell (ISC)-derived organoids provide key inroads into human epithelial biology6. However, intestinal organoids face limitations recapitulating intestinal physiology, owing to an inaccessible lumen, culture heterogeneity, lack of biomimetic morphology and absence of non-epithelial lineages7,8. Although bioengineered 3D extracellular matrix (ECM) scaffolds have helped to overcome some of these challenges by establishing crypt–villus architecture and apical–basal access9, physiological integration of epithelial, tissue-resident immune and microbial compartments remains a major challenge1,10.

Recent findings suggest that here we established engineered immunocompetent human intestinal models composed of autologous tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells and small intestinal or colonic ISC-derived epithelia amenable to luminal manipulation. Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) characterization of these barriers reveal region-specific spatial niches, mucus layer formation and immune–epithelium interactions. Applying this system to Salmonella Typhimurium (S.Tm), we provide a single-cell multiomic view of the epithelial responses to luminal and intracellular infection. Finally, we modelled the pathogen–epithelial–immune axis, demonstrating that TRM cells respond to S.Tm invasion by cytokine release and concomitant epithelial damage, which may facilitate pathogen clearance and infection resolution.

To model the human intestinal epithelium, we developed a fluidic device and microstamping technology to impart crypt-mimicking topography on an embedded ECM-like hydrogel (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Human intestinal organoids were seeded into the top reservoir of the device, where they formed a tight, polarized barrier comprising crypt units sustained by basal nutrition (Fig. 1a–d and Extended Data Fig. 1b–e).

To characterize the morphology, cellular composition and patterning of the epithelium, we developed a 3D-printed ‘histomold’ for simultaneous embedding and perpendicular sectioning of up to 50 engineered epithelia (Extended Data Fig. 1f). Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and mIF staining revealed histological and cell-type patterning similarity to donor-matched primary tissue (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Figs. 1g and 2a–c). In addition, a duodenal dual reporter line stably labelling chromatin (H2BC4–mTurquoise2) and LGR5+ stem cells (LGR5–IRES-NLS-mScarlet3) confirmed LGR5 ISC localization to the crypt bottom (Fig. 1f). By day 10, the thick epithelium contained proliferative SOX9+ and Ki67+ cells primarily confined to the crypt, whereas mature enterocytes (APOA4+ in the duodenum, and FABP6+ in the ileum) and colonocytes (CA1+) were enriched within inter-crypt regions (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 3a–f), with αDEF5+ Paneth cells detected in some small intestinal crypts (Extended Data Fig. 3g). EdU pulse-chase labelling revealed that cycling cells, initially localized in the crypt base, progressively migrated towards the apical surface over 4 days, similar to homeostatic turnover in vivo11 (Extended Data Fig. 3h and Supplementary Video 1). These data confirm that imposing in vivo-inspired geometries on human intestinal organoids drives reproducible cell-type regionalization and migration akin to the intestinal crypt–villus axis9.

Multiplexed scRNA-seq demonstrated region-specific stem, absorptive and secretory lineages across seven donors at day 10 (Fig. 1h–j, Extended Data Fig. 4a,b and Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Cell-type composition was similar to primary tissue counterparts and proportions were consistent across donors, highlighting the fidelity and robustness of the system (Fig. 1k and Extended Data Fig. 4c). Gene Ontology analysis of enterocyte and colonocyte marker genes revealed enrichment of distinct physiological programs concordant with the primary intestinal regions12,13 (Extended Data Fig. 4d and Supplementary Tables 3 and 4). Proximal small intestinal enterocytes demonstrated higher expression of genes involving lipid, xenobiotic and iron metabolism (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4d). Pseudotemporal ordering of the duodenal stem-to-enterocyte trajectory confirmed enterocyte maturation levels, approaching the AQP10+ expression observed at the villus tip in vivo14 (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Distal small intestinal enterocytes expressed bile acid and vitamin B12 transport genes, whereas colonocytes were enriched in cell–cell interactions and ion transport13,15 (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4d). We confirmed differential protein expression of the transporters SLC5A1, SLC10A2 and SLC26A2 between the regions (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 4f). Among secretory lineages, enteroendocrine cells and goblet cells were differentially abundant, with substantial heterogeneity in enteroendocrine cells (CHGA+) including EC (TPH1+), MX (GHRL+ and MLN+), D (SST+), K (GIP+), I (CCK+) and L (GCG+ and PYY+) subpopulations that match tissue distribution16 (Extended Data Figs. 2 and 4g–j).

Collectively, these data show that the engineered epithelium retains region-specific cell composition, spatial organization and gene expression, providing inroads to explore nutrient, xenobiotic and host–microbe processes in a human context.

The mucus, a layered network of mucins, cellular material, antimicrobials and structural factors, provides an interactive barrier between the microbiome and intestinal epithelium. Characterizing the properties and functional role of the mucus at the host–microbe interface remains largely under-explored in vitro. To facilitate rapid accumulation of mucus, we reduced the apical volume over the course of approximately 4 days, which resulted in a fibrous mucus network covering the epithelium (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 5a,b). Shed cells were present throughout the mucus layer, where they contribute to viscosity17 and can exert an antimicrobial role18 (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c). Longitudinal sections revealed an irregular mucus profile, with higher colonic thickness and crypt plumes similar to observations in primary tissue19 (Fig. 2c–e and Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). AlcianBlue–Periodic Acid–Schiff (PAS) co-staining showed regional differences in secretion and glycosylation, with higher ratios of acidic, negatively charged groups towards colon (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 5h,i). These patterns were comparable with the primary tissue and may be influenced by relative levels of fucose, sialic acid and sulfate groups20. Proteomic analysis of the colonic luminal content identified the core mucus layer proteins21 (MUC2, FCGBP, TFF3, AGR2, CLCA1, ZG16 and MUC5B) as major constituents, alongside additional mucins, antimicrobials and lectin-binding proteins (Fig. 2g, Extended Data Fig. 5j and Supplementary Table 5). Using the scRNA-seq data, we identified seven non-proliferative (MKI67−) goblet cell clusters (C0–C6) representing regional diversity and differentiation state (Fig. 2h, Extended Data Fig. 5k and Supplementary Table 3). Colonic goblet cells (C1) were enriched in intracellular vesicle transport, protein glycosylation and aerobic respiration, suggesting a higher secretion machinery consistent with thickness measurements (Extended Data Fig. 5l and Supplementary Table 4).

Next, we benchmarked the expression of membrane-bound mucins, key glycocalyx components that fortify the epithelium but remain difficult to recapitulate in vitro22. We observed a strong cell-type and region-specific gene expression comparable with the reference tissue (Fig. 2i). MUC6 and MUC5AC, which encode stomach mucins that are often expressed under pathological and metaplastic conditions23,24, were nearly absent. MUC12 and MUC17 staining in the engineered epithelium and tissue counterparts confirmed the specificity and maturation of the glycocalyx, revealing in vivo-like levels by day 12 of culture (Fig. 2j,k and Extended Data Fig. 5m). Finally, we functionally assessed the mucus upon colonization with the commensals Enterococcus faecium or Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus, which proliferated without compromising epithelial integrity (Fig. 2l and Extended Data Fig. 5n). Together, these results indicate that the platform can accumulate a complex mucus layer with in vivo-like and region-specific properties, opening new avenues for the study of human mucus and host–microbe interactions.

Sources indicate that unlike commensal microbiota, the foodborne pathogen S.Tm exploits motility and adhesion mechanisms to penetrate the mucus25, triggering an invasion-dependent inflammatory response that facilitates pathogen colonization26. Although extensive research has characterized the fundamental mechanisms underlying S.Tm infection, the exact epithelial responses and the resulting epithelial–immune signalling remain unresolved at the human level and at single-cell resolution.

Industry observers note that motivated by the higher mucus level and its potential role against pathogenic bacteria, we infected colonic epithelium with S.Tm 14028 in conditions with varying densities of mucus. At 18 h post-start of the infection (hpi), S.Tm triggered strong damage in conditions with less mucus (Mucuslo), whereas the epithelium remained largely unaffected in the presence of dense mucus (Mucushi; Fig. 3a–d and Extended Data Fig. 6a–d). Furthermore, the denser mucus led to a decrease in microbial burden, cell invasion and cytokine release, while preserving barrier integrity (Extended Data Fig. 6e–g). These protective effects were coupled with cell shedding, which predominantly localized at crypt openings, presumably impeding bacterial colonization (Extended Data Fig. 6h).

In a recent development, next, we used single-cell transcriptome and accessible chromatin sequencing (scMultiome) to characterize the Mucushi colonic epithelium response at 24 hpi and epithelial breach (Extended Data Fig. 6i). We detected canonical cell types in control and S.Tm conditions with increased proportion of mature colonocytes upon infection, a shift reported in mouse tissue27 (Fig. 3e,f and Extended Data Fig. 6j–l). Of note, ‘colonocyte subtype 1’ (RNA clusters C7-1 and C7-2) and ‘subtype 2’ (RNA cluster C8) were nearly exclusive to the infection condition (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6k). Overall, all cell types exhibited a pronounced response to infection with 3,056 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and 34,337 differentially accessible open chromatin regions (DARs) between conditions (Extended Data Fig. 6m–p and Supplementary Table 3). Pathway enrichment analysis highlighted hypoxia, NF-κB and barrier or cytoskeletal signatures, including upregulation of antimicrobials (LCN2 and PIGR), reactive oxygen species (DUOX2 and DUOXA2) and inflammatory cytokines (CCL20, IL18 and IL32; Extended Data Fig. 6q–s). Stem cells strongly upregulated LCN2, chemokines (CXCL1–3) and immunomodulators (TNF and LTB). Together, these results identify a complex innate epithelium response involving sensing, barrier maintenance and mucosal signalling.

It has been revealed that we used the chromatin accessibility data to infer a gene regulatory network underlying the epithelial response (Fig. 3g). This network revealed transcription factor nodes and target genes that orchestrate a broad-spectrum response, along with clusters that specifically coordinate infection-specific states. We identified BHLHE40, ZNF292 and RBPJ as the top differentially expressed transcription factors in the colonocyte subtype 1, which exhibited a hypoxic signature that appears conserved under infections and inflammatory-related diseases28. STAT3 emerged as a central node of the colonocyte subtype 2. Phosphorylation of STAT3 (pSTAT3) has been linked to intracellular S.Tm infection29 via the virulence factor SteE30,31, leading to an anti-inflammatory transcriptional program that supports the bacterial niche. Co-staining of pSTAT3 and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) revealed a strong colocalization both in colonic and small intestinal samples, with no pSTAT3 detection in non-infected conditions (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 7a–c). These results, in addition to the expression of the STAT3 negative-feedback regulator SOCS3, suggest that this population is S.Tm specific and contains cells with intracellular bacteria.

Finally, we classified DEGs into co-expression gene modules based on expression differences across cell types between conditions (Supplementary Table 3). We found that the colonocyte subtype 2-specific gene module exhibited increased reactive oxygen species, endoplasmic reticulum stress, unfolded protein response and ferroptosis (Extended Data Fig. 7d and Supplementary Table 4). Furthermore, we observed a possible antagonistic interaction between host cell and pathogen, with non-cannonical inflammasome signalling (CASP4, CASP5 and IL18)32 and genes with anti-inflammatory roles (SBNO2 and TNIP3; Extended Data Fig. 7e,f). BACH1, a key oxidative stress and ferroptosis regulator competing with NRF2 (NFE2L2)33,34, was also among the top upregulated transcription factors (Extended Data Fig. 7g). Binding motifs of STAT3 and BACH1 were over-represented in S.Tm DARs, indicating that both might be regulators of this population (Supplementary Table 6). Finally, we identified putative gene regulatory regions with increased accessibility upon infection, including intronic and distal regions of IL18 and SLC7A11 in the presumably invaded cells (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 7h). Collectively, these findings identify a complex multipartite human epithelial gene regulatory response to S.Tm infection, confirm STAT3 activation in S.Tm-invaded cells, and demonstrate how engineered intestines can be used to illuminate human infection responses.

Central to S.Tm pathogenesis resides a specialized virulence machinery including two needle-like type III secretion systems (T3SS-1/2) that mediate invasion and intracellular survival26,35 (Fig. 3j). To study how virulence factors influence the host response to luminal and intracellular S.Tm, we performed short, high-load infections (approximately 3 h, multiplicity of infection of approximately 1:60, −mucus) using wild-type (WT) and mutant strains. Subsequent gentamicin treatment removed the luminal stimulus while maintaining intracellular S.Tm populations for several days (Extended Data Fig. 8a).

Industry observers note that we observed that flagellum-driven motility (ΔfliC–ΔfljB (ΔFg)) contributed more to invasion than SiiE-dependent adhesion (ΔsiiF; Extended Data Fig. 8b). Consistent with our previous results (Extended Data Fig. 7a–c), internalized S.Tm predominantly localized basolaterally beneath the nucleus, presumably within Salmonella-containing vacuoles (SCV)35 (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Intracellular replication led to either cell extrusion events with luminal release or rupture of SCV-like structures that released S.Tm basally (Extended Data Fig. 8d and Supplementary Videos 2 and 3). The levels of IL-18 increased over 96 hpi and was a hallmark with WT but not avirulent ΔinvG–ΔssaV (ΔSPI-1/2) S.Tm, distinguishing this invasion signature from the broader luminal cytokine response (Fig. 3k and Extended Data Fig. 8e,f). In addition, the system demonstrated virulence sensitivity, as S.Tm SL1344 (ref. 36) elicited an exacerbated invasion-driven response marked by increased internalization, cell shedding and IL-18 secretion compared with S.Tm 14028 (Extended Data Fig. 8g).

To resolve host transcriptional responses induced by luminal or intracellular S.Tm, we performed scRNA-seq on GFP+ (invaded (In)) and GFP− (non-invaded (Out)) cells infected with WTGFP, ΔSPI-1/2GFP, ΔssaVGFP (ΔSPI-2) or ΔsteEGFP strains at 24 hpi (Fig. 3j,l and Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). Invasion occurred across all cell types but was lowest in stem cells, probably given their crypt-base localization (Extended Data Fig. 8j). The luminal response of non-invaded (GFP−) colonocytes was comparable between WT and ΔSPI-1/2, involving hypoxia, barrier and cytokine genes (Fig. 3m). A low-abundant colonocyte state appeared independent of invasion and was marked by IFN signalling (MX1 and ISG15), probably reflecting extracellular bacterial recognition37 (Fig. 3m, ‘depleted non-infected’, Extended Data Fig. 8i and Supplementary Table 4). The intracellular response of invaded (GFP+) colonocytes, which matched the colonocyte subtype 2 state from the multiomic analysis, triggered a profound shift (approximately 4,000 DEGs) characterized by pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory, bacterial recognition, cytoskeleton and oxidative stress genes with variable patterns along differentiation (Fig. 3m, Extended Data Fig. 8k,l and Supplementary Table 2). Although effector contributions may differ functionally, the attenuated gene signature observed in ΔSPI-2, and especially in ΔsteE-invaded cells, positions SteE as a key driver of the intracellular transcriptional landscape (‘enriched in GFP+’; Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 8i,l,m).

Among transcription factors, STAT3 (STAT3, SOCS3 and pSTAT3) was attenuated in ΔSPI-2 and absent in ΔsteE-invaded cells, confirming its SteE-mediated activation31 (Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 8l,n). Invasion by WT and mutants elicited coordinated upregulation of the antagonistic BACH1–NRF2 transcription factor pair33 that coincided with reduced expression of iron homeostasis regulators (GPX4, FTH1, HMOX1 and FTL), suggesting predominant BACH1 activity34 (Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 8l,o). SLC7A11 was a notable exception to this repression, possibly through non-canonical BACH1 activation34, STAT3 regulation38 or an alternative mechanism. Although the exact BACH1–NRF2 interplay and roles remain to be fully elucidated, these transcription factors appeared functionally coupled to intracellular S.Tm, as observed upon small-molecule inhibitor treatments (Extended Data Fig. 8p).

Finally, we classified S.TmWT-invaded cells by bacterial burden using imaging flow cytometry, identifying single-colony to high-load groups at 24 hpi (Extended Data Fig. 8q). To link intracellular replication levels to host response, we performed single-cell total RNA sequencing (VASA-seq) on index-sorted cells from GFPlo, GFPint and GFPhi levels (Extended Data Fig. 8r). GFPhi cells, with up to 35 colony-forming units (CFU) per cell, most strongly correlated with our previously defined intracellular gene module, linking the host response to S.Tm activity and replication rather than invasion alone (Extended Data Fig. 8s,t). Uniquely, VASA-seq recovered not only non-protein coding host transcripts but also bacterial genes involved in metabolism (mgtB, gltA and feoB) and SPI-2 machinery, highlighting the intracellular adaptation of the pathogen (Extended Data Fig. 8u,v and Supplementary Table 3). Collectively, these data provide a high-resolution, multi-modal atlas that uncovers how virulence factors and intracellular burden shape the invaded epithelial response.

Industry observers note that our transcriptomic analysis identified epithelial signals triggered by S.Tm infection and confirmed the epithelium as a sensor of pathogen presence. Elucidating the functional impact of these signals requires the presence of their target populations. Given that S.Tm infection was associated with induction of lymphocyte-targeting cytokines (IL-18 and TNF) and chemokines (CXCL10 and CCL20), we focused on T cells as putative responders and introduced them into the intestinal engineered tissues. In the human intestine, TRM cells reside within the mucosa to safeguard barrier integrity39. We have previously highlighted that TRM cells integrate into ISC-derived organoids and respond to synthetic T cell receptor (TCR) engagement40. Building on this approach, we established immunosurveilled barriers by incorporating autologous tissue-resident immune cells into the ECM scaffold of our engineered tissues (Fig. 4a–c and Extended Data Fig. 9a–c). These cells were isolated primarily from the small intestine due to higher proximal mucosal immune cell density5. We first assessed immune cell interactions with the epithelium, in the absence of a pathogenic threat. As expected from their tissue-resident phenotype facilitating epithelial interaction (Extended Data Fig. 9d–h), intraepithelial lymphocytes infiltrated the epithelium at physiological rates and patrolling speeds comparable with the organ of origin41 without compromising barrier integrity (Fig. 4d–i, Extended Data Fig. 9i,j and Supplementary Videos 4–6). By contrast, blood-derived T cells barely integrated into the epithelium (Fig. 4f).

To resolve the cellular diversity and epithelium–immune crosstalk, we performed scRNA-seq after 1 week of co-culture. The immune compartment exhibited striking heterogeneity, comprising CD8 T (CD8 TRM) cells, CD4 T helper (CD4 TRM) cells, regulatory T cells, T helper 17 (TH17 TRM) cells, γδ T cells, natural killer cells, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) and memory B cells (Fig. 4j), demonstrating maintenance of immune lineage fidelity (Extended Data Fig. 9k). TRM populations constituted the majority of the immune cell pool, remaining non-proliferative, consistent with their long-lived quiescent state in vivo42 (Fig. 4j and Extended Data Fig. 9d–g,k). Given their dominant representation, we refer to the entire immune compartment as ‘TRM cells’ henceforth. Although overall epithelial cell-type composition was unaffected (Fig. 4k and Extended Data Fig. 9l,m), immune cell presence induced epithelial antigen processing and presentation programs, marked by upregulation of MHC class I (MHC-I) components (HLA-B and B2M) and the MHC-II chaperone CD74 (Fig. 4l, Extended Data Fig. 9n–p and Supplementary Table 4). Transcription factor expression analysis in the enterocyte cluster linked gene expression changes to STAT1, IRF1 and IRF9, canonical hallmarks of IFNγ signalling (Fig. 4l), suggesting that immune-derived IFNγ facilitates this baseline immune priming43 (Fig. 4m). We confirmed IFNγ within culture supernatants at the protein level (Extended Data Fig. 9q).

Next, we found that engineered tissues recapitulate key epithelial–immune interactions, including IFNGR1/2–IFNG, IL15RA–IL15 (ref. 44) and TNFRSF14–CD160 (ref. 45) (Fig. 4m and Supplementary Table 7). Furthermore, introduction of resident immune cells drove upregulation of the butyrophilin-like (BTNL) molecules BTNL3 and BTNL8 within the epithelium, probably in a HNF4G-dependent manner46 (Fig. 4l). These epithelial BTNL molecules signal back to the immune compartment, facilitating maturation of Vγ4+ γδ T cells and establishing a protective mucosal circuit, whose disruption is linked to intestinal pathology47.

Together, these data suggest that engineered intestinal tissues preserve physiological immune cell behaviours and foster in vivo-like epithelial–immune interactions.

Having incorporated TRM cells into the engineered tissues, we next asked how they interpret epithelial-derived signals to orchestrate mucosal defence upon S.Tm infection. We challenged immunocompetent barriers with high-load S.Tm for 3 h following gentamicin treatment (Fig. 5a). Histological analysis confirmed bacteria within close proximity of intraepithelial lymphocytes (Fig. 5b). The presence of resident immune cells accelerated mucosal damage compared with epithelium-only controls, leading to increased epithelial shedding and loss of barrier integrity (Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 10a–c). Attributing elevated epithelial damage to TRM cell activation, we analysed the basal compartment for inflammatory mediators observed in patients with gastroenteric Salmonella infection48,49. We identified two temporally distinct regimes of immune and epithelial responses. A rapid (10 hpi) first wave of IL-2 and IFNγ secretion, indicating a canonical CD4+ TH1 response, occurred concurrently with epithelial secretion of IL-18 (Fig. 5d). This initial response was followed by release of cytotoxic and antimicrobial effectors, including GzmB, IL-6 and TH17-associated cytokines (IL17A and IL-22). TNF, IL-13 and IL-1β were modestly induced (Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 10d,e). Although facilitating pathogen clearance (Extended Data Fig. 10f), this TH1–TH17-driven TRM cell response was associated with mucosal injury.

To determine whether TRM cell activation requires epithelial invasion or only luminal exposure to the pathogen, we leveraged the S.Tm mutants introduced previously (ΔFg, ΔSPI-2 and ΔSPI-1/2; Fig. 3). We found that the extent of mucosal injury and the magnitude of TRM cell response correlated with S.Tm invasive capacity and epithelial IL-18 secretion (Fig. 5e,f and Extended Data Fig. 10g). Furthermore, in line with the stronger epithelial response described earlier (Extended Data Fig. 8g), S.Tm SL1344 induced a more rapid and severe immunopathology than S.Tm 14028 (Extended Data Fig. 10h). Together, these data link TRM cell responses to pathogen virulence, invasive capacity and subsequent epithelial cytokine secretion. Although TRM cell responses are classically defined by antigen-specific TCRs, their capacity for innate-like bystander responses is a critical yet poorly understood feature of human mucosal immunity. We sought to understand whether S.Tm-mediated TRM cell activation is driven by secreted epithelial signals rather than direct TCR binding to epithelial MHC. Inhibition of PI3K and p38 MAPK, essential for innate-like IFNγ induction50, significantly quelled the response, whereas TCR-dependent LCK inhibition51 showed no effect (Fig. 5g). Likewise, surface TCR expression remained stable during S.Tm infection, contrasting the expected downregulation triggered by synthetic TCR engagement via an EpCAM–CD3 bispecific52 (Fig. 5h). Conditioned media from infected epithelium-only barriers were sufficient to activate TRM cells, whereas direct stimulation with bacterial pathogen-associated molecular patterns (LPS and flagellin) failed to trigger degranulation (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 10i). We note that this non-cognate response appeared to be a hallmark of tissue residency, as allogeneic and autologous blood-derived T cells remained unresponsive to infection, despite exhibiting substantial CD45RO+ populations (Extended Data Fig. 9d), high viability and IL-2 induction capacity (Fig. 5i and Extended Data Fig. 10j,k). Together, these results establish S.Tm-induced TRM cell activation in this system as a TCR-independent bystander response that requires inflammatory signals relayed by the epithelium. The induction of IL-18 upon S.Tm invasion closely coincided with the kinetics of the T cell response (Fig. 5d), implicating this cytokine as a key epithelial orchestrator of T cell activation. This was supported by high expression of IL-18Rα on CD4+ TRM cells, which conferred pronounced responsiveness to exogenous IL-18 and S.Tm infection (Fig. 5j and Extended Data Fig. 10l,m). To assess its role as an epithelial messenger, we generated IL18 knockouts in intestinal organoids using CRISPR–Cas9, resulting in ablation of IL-18 expression at baseline and upon challenge (Fig. 5k and Extended Data Fig. 10n). Indeed, IL-18 levels in WT S.Tm-infected mutant barriers were comparable with those of the avirulent ΔSPI-1/2 infection and non-infected control (Fig. 5l). When assessing the TRM cell response, IL-18 deficiency significantly dampened the inflammatory response (Fig. 5l,m), attenuating intracellular IFNγ levels in the cytotoxic IL-18Rα+CD4+ responder population (Extended Data Fig. 10o). Critically, the loss of IL-18 protected the barrier from pathological shedding and thinning (Fig. 5n and Extended Data Fig. 10p) despite functional T cell responder potential, linking IL-18-driven T cell activation to immunopathology.

Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the epithelium orchestrates antibacterial mucosal defence by secreting IL-18 to trigger non-cognate, innate-like responses of the TRM compartment.

Sources indicate that we have reported bioengineered, luminally accessible human intestinal tissues comprising epithelia with periodically repeating crypts that maintain LGR5+ stem cells, in vivo-like cell composition and patterning, and retain transcriptomic signatures across multiple donors. Identical medium and biophysical culture conditions yield region-specific signatures due to stem cell origin. Cell-type maturation and a reduction in total apical volume enable the formation of a region-specific mucus layer with mature glycocalyx. In addition, autologous TRM cells patrol the barrier and engage in bidirectional crosstalk with the epithelium, conferring an immune-responsive state within epithelial cells via IFNγ signalling.

The modularity of the system enabled upcoming inquiry into S.Tm infection in a human context, contributing to collective efforts to refine physiologically relevant enteric infection models53. Basolateral S.Tm localization within polarized cells presumably facilitates dissemination into the lamina propria, a phenomenon that has been reported in vivo54,55. In addition, the phenotypic divergence observed between SL1344 and 14028 strains could expand to clinical isolates and human-restricted pathogens (for example, Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhi, Shigella flexneri and Vibrio cholerae), including the study of host factors influencing bacterial gene expression and antibiotic susceptibility. We mapped the gene regulatory networks underlying luminal and intracellular S.Tm at single-cell resolution. The epithelium orchestrated inflammatory, metabolic and structural responses that accompany S.Tm colonization26 and demonstrate an innate-sensing capacity that coordinates multi-lineage immune recruitment in vivo. S.Tm invasion reshaped the host transcriptome through a SteE-dependent STAT3 gene regulatory hub that extends results in macrophages and immortalized lines29,31. The reduced SPI-2 contribution may stem from non-transcriptional effector roles or delayed activation resulting from the SPI-1-inducing pre-culture protocol56. In addition, changes in oxidative stress and iron homeostasis suggest a host–pathogen interplay associated with other intracellular infections57, warranting further study. Overall, these responses were highly influenced by the intracellular burden of the pathogen.

Advancing our previous work40 to an apically accessible immunocompetent system, we demonstrated that epithelial IL-18 upon S.Tm invasion is sufficient to drive TRM cell activation and cytokine release, reflecting clinical gastroenteric salmonellosis48,49. The system allowed us to elucidate the functional effects of this bystander T cell activation, aligning with previous reports of innate-like polyfunctional capabilities of TRM cells58,59,60. TRM cells intensified infection-mediated epithelial shedding, which probably contributes to pathogen clearance61 and is consistent with the rapid onset of diarrhoea during S.Tm infection. Although mouse studies have established the necessity of IL-18 for CD4+ T cell defence upon S.Tm infection62, it has been shown that enteric neurons, rather than the epithelium, serve as the critical source of IL-18 for intestinal protection63. We demonstrated that the human intestinal epithelium can potently activate TRM cells via IL-18 to drive defence responses, at least in an in vitro setting. Of note, S.Tm infection64 and IL-18 (ref. 65) have been linked to the onset of inflammatory bowel disease. Our data raise the possibility that this association may be underpinned by the appearance of a cytotoxic IL-18Rα+CD4+ T cell population58,62.

Although our platform provides a unique window into human intestinal in vitro modelling, several limitations remain. The engineered tissues lack villous structures, specialized Paneth or M cells, and myeloid immune lineages, crucial mediators of immunity against infection. The lack of fluid exchange might affect biophysical characteristics of a mucus layer accumulated by apical media reduction. Furthermore, S.Tm invasion rates probably exceed physiological levels due to mucus protection. Future studies may circumvent these limitations through bioengineering approaches9, mucus secretagogues, cytokine supplementation or the inclusion of additional commensal and immune lineages.

Beyond host–pathogen interaction, the engineered tissues and analytical framework expand what can be addressed ex vivo. The mature, patterned epithelium opens research directions in region-specific drugs and nutrient absorption, mucus biology and epithelial–TRM cell interactions implicated in inflammatory bowel disease pathogenesis. Overall, the platform brings the field closer to capturing complex, organ-level processes in a human setting that is controllable and tractable.

Consenting patients underwent visceral surgery with partial resection of intestine (precise intestinal regions are listed in Supplementary Table 1) for various oncological indications. We used microscopically and/or macroscopically tumour-free regions of resectates for further preparation and downstream handling. During the work on this project, a large number of microdevice prototype versions were fabricated using a range of microfabrication techniques, including cleanroom soft lithography, 3D printing, two-photon polymerization (2PP) lithography, computer numerical control (CNC) milling and plastic injection molding. The final chip is designed in a slide format (75 × 25 mm) containing three independent chips per slide. Each chip contained a central hydrogel chamber flanked by two side medium reservoirs and one top medium reservoir. The hydrogel precursor was injected through a loading port leading to the central gel chamber. A cylindrical stamp with a microtopography (for example, an array of biomimetic micropillars) on its base was placed onto a stamp-holding edge of the top reservoir before gel injection. After gel polymerization (see details in a separate section), the stamp was removed, leaving an inverse microtopography (for example, an array of microwells) on the hydrogel surface. The top and side reservoirs were then filled with PBS or cell culture medium. The top reservoir was used for cell seeding and subsequently served as the apical medium reservoir after epithelial coverage of the hydrogel and barrier formation. Medium from the side reservoirs passively diffused through the gel, supplying the epithelial tissue with nutrients from the basal side. Early prototypes were fabricated using conventional soft lithography and polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) molding workflows established at the Center of Micronanotechnology (EPFL). The 3D chip design was split into two photomasks that were sequentially aligned to enable the creation of pseudo-3D features and different heights for phase-guiding micro-pillars. Chip layouts were patterned onto chrome-coated fused silica substrates via laser lithography (VPG200, Heidelberg Instruments). Three layers of SU8 GM1075 (Gerlteltec) were sequentially spin coated onto dehydrated silicon wafers to achieve a total mold thickness of 750 μm. The first two 250-μm layers were soft baked, exposed to UV through the first photomask (MA6/BA6, Süss MicroTec) and post-baked. Then, the third SU8 layer was spin coated, soft baked and the second photomask was aligned to the existing pattern using dedicated alignment marks. After a final post-exposure bake and development with propylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate (PGMEA; Sigma), the molds were hard baked at 135 °C for 4 h and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS (Sylgard 184, Dow Corning) was mixed at a 10:1 base-to-curing agent ratio, poured onto the molds, degassed under vacuum and cured at 80 °C for 24 h. PDMS replicas were cut, punched and plasma bonded to glass-bottom dishes. The strength of the soft lithography pipeline is in fabrication of high-resolution microfeatures and with relatively optimal throughput, as 10–20 chips can be produced from a single wafer. However, fabrication of the models taller than 500 μm is challenging and only step-like, pseudo-3D features from a single side of the PDMS layer can be fabricated. To overcome these limitations, we explored several other complementary fabrication strategies. Commercial 3D-printing techniques such as fused deposition modelling and stereolithography were used for the production of larger models (Formlabs Form 4). However, these methods lacked the resolution and surface finish required for high-quality PDMS molding and were suitable only for some early-stage proof-of-concept prototypes. Instead, here we used 2PP lithography using the UpNano NanoOne printer to fabricate detailed 3D features of the chip. In brief, 3D models of the microchip were created in Autodesk Fusion (latest version), exported as STL files and processed using UpNano Think3D software. The models were printed on glass coverslips using UpPhoto resin (UpNano). NanoOne stands out as the most developed printer for mesoscale manufacturing, enabling printing of large structures (10–20 mm in xy and up to 40 mm in height) due to several advanced technologies: a submerged printing mode in a large resin reservoir, high-power 1,000 W, 780-nm laser for fast printing with 5 × 0.25 numerical aperture (NA) objective and adaptive resolution technology that significantly reduces print times (up to 450 mm3 h−1). After printing, the coverslips were washed in isopropanol and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS was cast, degassed, cured at 80 °C and then replicas were cut and plasma bonded to glass-bottom dishes. This method allowed us to fabricate high-quality prototypes for validation of the 3D microstructural design elements. However, the main limitation is the upscaling technology for fabrication of the large number of chips. More importantly, process flow is still resulting in the 3D topography features only from one side of the PDMS replica. To overcome the latter problem, commonly some laboratories fabricate multi-layered PDMS chips. In this approach, individual PDMS layers are fabricated separately, aligned and plasma bonded together. This direction was explored early on for fabrication of a few prototypes; however, the alignment process is tedious and unsuitable for large-scale chip manufacturing with the acceptable quality. To address this, inspired by industrial injection molding technology, we developed a cassette mold for PDMS curing. Molds were manufactured by CNC milling of acrylic, aluminum or steel, depending on the desired feature size and quality. Each cassette consisted of two mold parts bearing microtopographies of the bottom and top surfaces of the chip. When assembled, the parts fit precisely, enabling accurate alignment of both sides of the device. PDMS was injected into centre space of the mold, degassed in a vacuum chamber and cured in an 80 °C oven. After curing, the mold was opened and the PDMS sheets were cut and bonded to glass-bottom dishes. This process overcomes many of the limitations of previously described techniques and enables scalable production of hundreds of high-quality chips in a single batch. The main drawback is the need to adapt design features for CNC milling: some of the smallest features must be enlarged and sharp corners rounded. However, we did not consider this as a drawback as concurrently we began exploring industrial plastic molding technologies to eliminate the last remaining problem: the PDMS material itself. Although PDMS is ideal for prototyping, its high absorption of small molecules makes it unsuitable for translational applications and drug testing. Many of the learnings and design optimizations from the PDMS cassette-molding process were directly translated into the design of the final injection-molded plastic chip. Right now, the chip body is fabricated from cyclic olefin copolymer (COC) due to its low shrinkage, chemical resistance and optical transmission. The main body was fabricated as a single piece, followed by bonding of a 170-μm COC film to the bottom surface. A matching lid converting the slide was later designed and produced separately also via a COC injection molding process. After assembly, chips were packaged and sterilized using ethylene oxide gas. Large-scale chip production was outsourced to an external manufacturing facility.

Stamps featuring crypt-mimicking microtopography were fabricated from PDMS via replica molding of 2PP-printed models. First, arrays of colon crypt-mimicking micropillars were designed in Autodesk Fusion (latest version). Several topographies were tested and optimized, the final microtopography design consisted of the slightly conical pillars, ranging from 70 to 120 μm in diameter (top to bottom) and 700 μm in height. The 3D model was printed using a NanoOne (UpNano) 2PP printer on glass coverslips with UpPhoto resin and a 10 × 0.4 NA objective. To generate a master mold with inverted topography, the printed structures were plasma activated and silanized overnight using vapour-phase trichloro(1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorooctyl) silane (Sigma-Aldrich). PDMS (Sylgard 184, Dow Corning; 10:1 base-to-curing agent ratio) was poured over the master, degassed under vacuum and cured at 80 °C for 12 h. The resulting PDMS replica was cut, plasma activated and silanized overnight as above. This PDMS negative was then used repeatedly as a mold for casting final PDMS stamps using the same procedure (Sylgard 184, 10:1 ratio, cured at 80 °C for 12 h).

To generate the ECM for the chip bovine TeloCol-6 type I collagen solution (5225-50 ml, Advanced Biomatrix) was neutralized following the manufacturer’s instructions and then mixed with Matrigel (356231, Corning) in 87.5:12.5 (v/v) ratio. A PDMS stamp with crypt-mimmicking array of pillar topography was placed in the central top reservoir. After the gel injection through the gel-loading port, the hydrogel was polymerized on a 37 °C hotplate for 10 min. After ECM polymerization, all chip reservoirs were topped up with PBS or cell culture medium. Prepared chips with hydrogels can be stored for multiple weeks at 37 °C at 5% CO2 (hereafter referred to as ‘incubator’) or in the +4 °C fridge before use. Hydrogel stiffness was measured using an MCR 702e MultiDrive oscillatory shear rheometer (Anton Paar) in a parallel plate configuration with a PP25/P3 measuring plate. The Young’s modulus (E) was estimated from the storage modulus (G′), assuming the hydrogel is elastic and nearly incompressible, using the relation E = 2 G(1 + ν) ≈ 3 G′, where Poisson’s ratio (ν) is approximately 0.5. Across multiple batches and replicates, the hydrogels yielded a Young’s modulus of 3,000 ± 500 Pa.

In brief, intestinal tissue was processed by removal of the underlying muscularis, serosa and fat from the basal side of the intestinal tissue using forceps and scissors. The remaining mucosal tissue was thoroughly washed with DPBS (10010-015, Gibco), supplemented with penicillin–streptomycin (1,500 U ml−1; 15140122, Gibco), gentamicin (500 µg ml−1; 15750060, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and primocin (50 µg ml−1; ant-pm1, Invivogen) before using a glass coverslip to remove excess mucus from the luminal side and blood vessels from the basal side.

It has been revealed that to circumvent the poor viability and phenotypic alterations associated with traditional enzymatic disassociations66,67, we adapted and optimized a scaffold-based egression method68 that we have previously shown maximizes tissue-resident immune cell recovery and maintains phenotypic integrity40. As previously reported40, our characterization via scRNA-seq and flow cytometry analysis showed that the vast majority of the isolated cells are TRM cells. Therefore, we used the term TRM cells to describe the total immune cell fraction isolated from intestinal tissue. By flow cytometry, we characterized them as TRM cells based on the assessment of one or multiple of the following markers CD45RO+, CD69+, CD103+, CD45RA− and CCR7−.

Sources indicate that cleaned tissue was cut into square pieces (approximately 5 × 5 mm3) with a scalpel. Next, each fragment was loaded onto a 9 × 9 × 1.5 mm3 tantalum-coated, carbon-based scaffold (MSPP23281-1-REV-A, Ultramet) and cultured in 24-well plates (CC7682-7524, CytoOne) containing 2 ml of cytokine-free immune medium (Supplementary Table 1). Twenty-four hours later, scaffolds with tissue on were removed, and egressed cells were harvested from the bottom of the wells by thorough pipetting. Cells were then counted and biobanked in CryoStor (C2874, Sigma-Aldrich) before further use.

Recent findings suggest that for isolation of donor-matched crypts for organoid establishment, an adjacent clean tissue piece (approximately 3 cm2) was used. Intestinal villi were removed from the tissue by using a glass coverslip. The tissue was then incubated on ice in DPBS + 10 mM EDTA (15575020, Thermo Fisher Scientific) on a shaker for 30 min. Next, a coverslip was used to scrape off the crypts of the tissue. Crypts were collected in organoid medium (Supplementary Table 1). Crypts were centrifuged and resuspended in GFR Matrigel (356231, Corning). After polymerization for 15 min at 37 °C, organoid medium was added with 10 µm Y-27632 (72305, Stemcell Technologies). Following organoid formation, organoids were passaged every 7 days (up to a maximum of 25 passages). After three passages, organoid mycoplasma tests (LT07-710, Lonza) were performed. All lines used in this study were verified as negative for mycoplasma. Organoid banking was performed using CELLBANKER 1 (11888, Nippon Zenyaku Kogyo). Passaging was performed as previously described52. In brief, organoid medium was removed and wells were washed with DPBS. Next, 500 µl of Gentle Cell Dissociation reagent (07174, Stemcell Technologies) was added and incubated for 2 min at room temperature before collecting the domes in a Falcon tube. After a further 15 min of incubation at room temperature, the suspension was centrifuged at 350g at 4 °C for 5 min. After removal of liquid, the pellet was harshly resuspended with organoid wash medium (Supplementary Table 1) to break the organoids. Broken organoids were centrifuged at 500g and the supernatant discarded before pellet resuspension in GFR Matrigel.

In a recent development, to generate LGR5, CDH1 and H2BC4 reporter lines, targeting vectors were designed as previously described69. Human intestinal organoids were incubated with 1.25% DMSO (v/v) and 10 µM Y-27632 (72305, Stemcell Technologies) 24 h before electroporation. Organoids (amounting to approximately 1 million cells per condition) were harvested, dissociated to clumps of 3–5 cells with TrypLE (12604-013, Gibco), washed twice with Optimem (31985070, Gibco) and then resuspended in High Performance Electroporation Solution (45-0805, BTXpress) containing up to 10 µg of targeting vector and 10 µg of Cas9 and guide RNA-expressing vector. Cells were electroporated using the NEPA21 Super Electroporator (Nepagene) with settings as previously described70. Y-27632 was kept for 48 h post-single-cell seeding in growth factor-reduced Matrigel (356231, Corning). Reporter-positive organoids were either picked manually or enriched via FACS.

It has been revealed that to generate IL-18 gene knockouts, cells were transfected with 20 µg Cas9–GFP and guide RNA expression constructs at a 1:8 ratio and incubated overnight in culture medium containing 5% Matrigel. Transfected cells were FACS enriched and allowed to grow for 10–14 days. Up to eight clones were manually picked and genotyped by Sanger sequencing of the targeted locus.

Sources indicate that S.Tm NCTC 12023 (identical to ATCC14028) and SL1344 WT and isogenic mutant strains were used as listed in Supplementary Table 1. If required for detection of Salmonella by GFP expression, plasmid pFPV25.1 was introduced by electroporation and maintained by selection with 50 µg ml−1 carbenicillin (Roth).

Sources indicate that mutant strains with deletion in invG or steE were generated by λ-Red recombination as previously described71 using pKD13 as template for amplification with Del13 primer sets (synthesized by IDT) listed in Supplementary Table 1, and pWRG730 for expression for λ-Red recombinase functions72. Proper insertion of the aph resistance cassette in target genes was confirmed by colony PCR using DelCheck for primers and K1 Red-Del. If required, the aph resistance cassette was removed by FLP recombination mediated by helper plasmid pE-FLP73. Resulting clones were checked for loss of kanamycin resistance and pE-FLP, and FLP-mediated deletion was confirmed by colony PCR using DelCheck For/Rev primer sets.

Sources indicate that strain MvP3487 was generated by P22 transduction of the ΔssaV::aph allele into MvP1764 according to standard procedures. Resulting mutant strains were checked for the absence of lysogens.

It has been revealed that for seeding of the chips—hereafter referred to as ‘engineered intestines’ once intestinal epithelial cells are included—approximately 4-day-old human intestinal organoids from different regions of the gastrointestinal tract (duodenum, jejunum, ileum and colon) between passages 5 and 25 were collected in base medium (Supplementary Table 1) and transferred to a 15-ml Falcon tube. Following centrifugation at 300g at 4 °C for 4 min, the base medium was aspirated and the pellet was thoroughly resuspended in base medium. After repeating the centrifugation step, organoids were singularized with TrypLE express solution (12604-013, Gibco) containing 250 U ml−1 DNase I (4536282001, Roche) and 10 µm Y-27632 (72305, Stemcell Technologies) for 8 min at 37 °C before harsh resuspension. This step was performed twice before swiftly blocking the dissociation by adding base medium with 10% FBS. Next, cells were passed through a 40-µm strainer (43-50040-51, PluriSelect) before centrifugation at 500g at 4 °C for 4 min. Afterwards, the cells were resuspended in chip medium (Supplementary Table 1) containing 10 µm Y-27632. Approximately 1.5 × 105 cells were seeded in a volume of 3 µl onto each micropatterned hydrogel. Approximately 150 µl chip medium with 10 µm Y-27632 was immediately added to each side reservoir of the engineered intestines, whereas the mid-chamber remained empty to allow the cells to attach to the ECM. After 30 min in the incubator, 100 µl chip medium (+10 µm Y-27632 + 5% FBS) was carefully added to the mid-chamber to avoid cell detachment. Culture medium was exchanged every second day. Approximately 5% of FBS supplementation was removed after the second day (details in Supplementary Table 1).

On the day of hydrogel seeding, TRM cells or peripheral blood mononuclear cells were thawed following our previously described protocol52. T cells were isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells using the EasySep Human T Cell Isolation kit (17951, Stemcell Technologies) and EasySep Magnet (18000, Stemcell Technologies) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Viability and number of immune cells were assessed with Trypan Blue (216040, Invitrogen) on a Countess II (Invitrogen). If the viability of the thawed TRM cells crawl-out was less than 75% (due to remaining tissue debris), Dead Cell Removal Kit (130-090-101, Miltenyi Biotec) was applied with MS columns (130-042-201, Miltenyi Biotec) on the OctoMACS separator (130-042-109, Miltenyi Biotec) following the manufacturer’s instructions (typically improved to more than 85% viability). Afterwards, immune cells were placed in the incubator until further processing. Chips were prepared as described above until hydrogel loading. Then, approximately 1 × 105 immune cells were mixed with 6 µl of ECM per chip. Next, 26 µl of ECM was dispensed through the loading port per chip into the mid-reservoir. Immediately after, 6 µl of the ECM-immune suspension was carefully dispensed onto a flipped PDMS stamp, with the micropattern facing upwards, and transferred using forceps onto the previously dispensed ECM in the mid-reservoir of the engineered intestine. Next, immune-hydrogel suspensions were polymerized at 37 °C for 15 min. After polymerization of the ECM, the immune chip slide was topped up with immune chip medium (Supplementary Table 1) to ease microstamp removal. After organoid dissociation and epithelial cell seeding as described above, 150 µl immune chip medium containing 500 pg ml−1 IL-15 (570306, BioLegend) and 10 µm Y-27632 was immediately added to each side reservoir of the engineered intestine, whereas the mid-chamber remained empty to allow for cells to attach to the ECM of the engineered intestine. After 30 min in the incubator, 100 µl immune chip medium (+500 pg ml−1 IL-15 + 10 µm Y-27632) was carefully added to the mid-chamber. Immune chip medium (+500 pg ml−1 IL-15) was exchanged every second day.

Sources indicate that to assess the effects of bacterial components on TRM cells in suspension, LPS (100 ng ml−1; L3024-5MG, Sigma-Aldrich) and flagellin (50 ng ml−1; tlrl-epstfla-5, InvivoGen) were supplemented in immune medium and cultured for 48 h. Similarly, IL-15 (500 pg ml−1) and IL-18 (10 ng ml−1; 592106, BioLegend) were added in immune medium for TRM cell suspension cultures, either individually or in combination, for 48 h. For the assessment of T cell activation in response to the epithelial secretome, conditioned medium was harvested from the basal reservoirs of epithelium-only chips 48 hpi with S.Tm. This medium was collected, transferred to plates and maintained at −80 °C until the day of the experiment. Upon thawing, condition medium was mixed 1:1 (v/v) with fresh immune medium supplemented with 1,000 pg ml−1 of IL-15, resulting in a final concentration of 500 pg ml−1 of IL-15. TRM cells were subsequently cultured in this mixture for 48 h in suspension. Following these culture periods, cells were subjected to analysis by flow cytometry.

Industry observers note that for baseline phenotyping, immune cells were recovered from intestinal resections, filtered through a 40-µm strainer and processed directly. For assessment of luminal content, cells were recovered from the accessible luminal reservoir of the chips. For chip-harvested samples and suspension-cultured TRM cells intended for intracellular cytokine assessment, samples were treated with a protein transport inhibitor cocktail (00-4975-93, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 4 h before harvest. To achieve single-cell suspension of tissues for staining, samples were retrieved via a 3-mm biopsy punch and transferred to warm RPMI supplemented with L-glutamine (1X), 5% FBS, HEPES (1X), DNAse I (40 U ml−1), collagenase D (2 mg ml−1; 11088858001, Millipore) and trypsin inhibitor (1 mg ml−1; T9128, Sigma). Samples were incubated in a shaker (1,000 rpm at 37 °C) for 10 min with mechanical dissociation via vigorous pipetting every 3 min. Following visible disintegration, cells were centrifuged (500g for 3 min), resuspended in Accutase with DNAse I (40 U ml−1) and incubated for 10 min at room temperature until a single-cell suspension was achieved. All samples were filtered (40 µm) and washed twice in FACS buffer (DPBS supplemented with 2 mM EDTA and 2% FBS) before staining.

Recent findings suggest that cells were incubated with True-FcX (1:200; 422302, BioLegend) in Brilliant Stain Buffer (566385, BD Biosciences) for 10 min at room temperature in PBS, followed by a fixable viability dye in PBS (00-4975-93, Thermo Fisher) for 10 min following centrifugation. Surface antibodies were applied in FACS buffer for 15 min at room temperature. Following centrifugation and surface labelling, samples were processed according to their experimental requirement. Baseline samples were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 30 min at room temperature. Intracellular cytokine samples were fixed using IC fixation buffer (30 min in the dark at room temperature; 15284728, Invitrogen), washed in 1X permeabilization buffer (15284728, Invitrogen) and incubated with intracellular antibodies for 30 min at room temperature. Finally, samples were washed once more in 1X permeabilization buffer before centrifugation.

Cells were incubated with True-FcX (1:200; 422302, BioLegend) and brilliant stain buffer (566385, BD Biosciences) in FACS buffer for 15 min at 4 °C. Without washing, a 2X concentrated antibody master mix of chemokine receptors (CX3CR1, CXCR5, CCR7 and CD103) was added directly and incubated for 20 min at 37 °C in the incubator. Following centrifugation, the remaining surface antibodies and streptavidin were applied in FACS buffer for 20 min at 4 °C, followed by a single wash with PBS and centrifugation. Viability dye was then added in PBS for 20 min at 4 °C, followed by centrifugation. To fix and permeabilize the cells for intracellular cytokine and transcription factor staining, the FoxP3 kit (00-5523-00, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used according to the manufacturer’s instructions (30 min at 4 °C). Following centrifugation, intracellular antibodies were prepared in 1X permeabilization buffer and incubated for 30 min at 37 °C. Finally, samples were washed twice in 1X permeabilization buffer before the final centrifugation and acquisition.

Final cell suspensions were resuspended in 150 µl FACS buffer and acquired on a BD Fortessa or a Cytek Aurora (five-laser configuration). Data were analysed using FlowJo (v10; BD Biosciences) and OMIQ (v1.22; Dotmatics). All surface and intracellular staining antibodies can be found in Supplementary Table 1.

From the raw data acquired by flow cytometry, using FlowJo software (v10.10; BD Biosciences), live CD45+ cells were identified using manual gating. For flow-cytometry data, the compensation matrix was corrected in FlowJo (BD Biosciences) by pre-gating on live immune cells, and the total fraction of live singlet immune cells was exported. Data were then transformed with an inverse hyperbolic sine (arcsinh) function (cofactors ranging between 400 and 10,000), then imported into the OMIQ environment (v1.22; Dotmatics) for subsequent analysis.

The high-dimensional analysis was carried out based on the workflow previously described74. In brief, UMAPs75 were generated, and FlowSOM clustering76 was overlaid on the dimensionality reduction maps. Frequency plots were generated downstream of manual gating outputs using Prism (v10.6.1).

Industry observers note that to assess the barrier integrity of the engineered epithelia in homeostatic conditions, the apical and basal media were aspirated thoroughly. Next, 120 µl of a 100 µg ml−1 solution of Cascade Blue hydrazide, trilithium salt (C3239, Invitrogen) in chip medium (Supplementary Table 1) was added to the apical reservoir. Of chip medium without Cascade Blue, 170 µl was added to the side reservoirs. The assay was carried out for 180 min in the incubator. Subsequently, the fluorescence of the basal medium was quantified using Cell Culture Microplates (655090, Greiner Bio-one) in the Flex Station 3 plate reader (Molecular Devices), with measurements taken from the top at an excitation wavelength of 380 nm and an emission wavelength of 420 nm using the software SoftMax Pro (v7.2). The concentration of Cascade Blue that diffused to the basal compartment was calculated against a standard curve and the resulting apparent permeability (Papp) was quantified using the following formula:.

where Vbasal is the volume of the basal compartment, dCbasal is the measured concentration in the basal compartment, A is the area of the epithelial monolayer grown on the ECM (0.19477 cm2), dt is the time of the assay and Capical, t = 0 is the initial concentration added to the apical reservoir at the start of the assay. For infection experiments, one gentle DPBS wash was performed in the apical reservoir of control and infected samples to remove the majority of the grown biofilm before permeability assessment. The Cascade Blue, in addition to 200 µg ml−1 of gentamicin (G1397-10ML, Sigma-Aldrich), were supplemented in the chip medium. The assay was conducted over a period of 90 min, and fluorescence was measured from the bottom using a cell culture microplate that was covered with a transparent adhesive foil on top.

The accumulation of mucus was facilitated by reducing the total apical volume from approximately 120 to 100 µl of chip medium (Supplementary Table 1) to either approximately 30 µl or about 5 µl, based on the experimental needs.
