Hull City vs. Brighton: Head-to-head record and past meetings before Premier League clash

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Seye Omidiora | 20 Nov 2026 13:39.
  • Second-placed Brighton & Hove Albion travel to face Hull City on Sunday as Fabian Hurzeler's side look to extend their impressive run of form in the clubs' first-ever Premier League meeting.
  • Sergej Jakirovic's Tigers sit 13th after 10 matches and three points clear of the relegation zone, having gone eight league games without a victory despite remaining unbeaten on home soil this season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Seye Omidiora | 20 Nov 2026 13:39.

Second-placed Brighton & Hove Albion travel to face Hull City on Sunday as Fabian Hurzeler's side look to extend their impressive run of form in the clubs' first-ever Premier League meeting.

Sergej Jakirovic's Tigers sit 13th after 10 matches and three points clear of the relegation zone, having gone eight league games without a victory despite remaining unbeaten on home soil this season.

Conversely, the Seagulls arrive full of confidence after recording consecutive top-flight wins over Manchester City and Brentford, boasting six clean sheets across their last seven league outings.

Here, Sports Mole takes a closer look at the head-to-head record and past meetings between Hull and Brighton.

Nearly 67 years have passed since Hull City and Brighton & Hove Albion first locked horns - a November 1959 Division Two clash that ended in a 3-1 victory for the Tigers - and there have now been 51 competitive meetings between the two clubs in all competitions.

The Seagulls hold the bragging rights when it comes to overall victories with 22, while Hull have claimed 15 wins of their own and another 14 contests have seen the spoils shared.

Remarkably, none of those 51 encounters have taken place in the Premier League, with every previous battle arriving in the Football League or the FA Cup, and the two sides have not crossed paths since a goalless Championship stalemate in East Yorkshire in February 2016.

Recent clashes between the pair have been notably tight, low-scoring affairs, with none of their last nine meetings across all competitions settled by more than a single goal and three ending 0-0.

During the 2015-16 campaign, both clubs collected a narrow 1-0 victory on home soil - Brighton prevailing in the Championship in September 2015 before Hull gained revenge in the FA Cup four months later - prior to that goalless draw in February.

Indeed, home advantage has heavily dictated this fixture in the modern era, as Hull are unbeaten in their last six home games against Brighton across all competitions - winning four and keeping five clean sheets - since suffering a 2-0 Division Three defeat in October 2000.

Conversely, the Tigers have endured a miserable record on the South Coast, failing to win any of their last 22 visits to Brighton since recording their sole away triumph in this fixture - a 2-1 Division Three success - way back in August 1965.

Brighton built much of their overall head-to-head lead during a dominant spell in the late 1980s and 1990s, rattling off four straight victories between October 1989 and April 1991 before later embarking on a nine-match unbeaten run from April 1993 to December 1996.

That sequence included the Seagulls' biggest-ever win in this matchup, a resounding 4-0 Division Two triumph in March 1996, while they also completed a comfortable league double over Hull with 2-0 and 3-0 victories in the 2000-01 Division Three season.

Hull's most emphatic triumph came in the highest-scoring meeting between the two sides, a 5-2 Division Two victory in December 1988, while they also put three unanswered goals past Brighton in March 1997.

The two teams have also collided five times in the FA Cup, with Brighton winning the first two ties in January 1985 (1-0) and January 1986 (3-2) before Hull turned the tide by edging a 2-1 replay victory in February 2014 following a 1-1 draw and claiming that 1-0 success in January 2016.

Jan 09, 2016: Hull City 1-0 Brighton (FA Cup).

Sep 12, 2015: Brighton 1-0 Hull City (Championship).

Feb 24, 2014: Hull City 2-1 Brighton (FA Cup).

Feb 17, 2014: Brighton 1-1 Hull City (FA Cup).

Feb 09, 2013: Brighton 1-0 Hull City (Championship).

Aug 18, 2012: Hull City 1-0 Brighton (Championship).

Feb 22, 2012: Hull City 0-0 Brighton (Championship).

Oct 15, 2011: Brighton 0-0 Hull City (Championship).

Dec 16, 2005: Brighton 2-1 Hull City (Championship).

Mar 10, 2001: Brighton 3-0 Hull City (League Division Three).

Sources indicate that sometimes comments, however over the top, hit home. Michael Carrick will desperately hope the remark from his former Manchester United team-mate Gary Neville is not one of them. That it does not stick. That it does not come to define his time in charge of United this season – if he lasts this season. Or be used in one of those highlight reels, with doom-laden music, to explain the story of this Premier League campaign.

Sources indicate that on TV co-commentary duty for Sky, Neville referred to United as “blue mannequins” (they were wearing their away kit) and said that for a period after half-time it was the worst he had ever seen them play since he started watching, aged five. Neville is now 51. That is a lot of games to settle on this conclusion so strongly and, surely, inaccurately.

Sources indicate that "They were absolutely mannequins!" Gary Neville indicates Michael Carrick has to stop defending the Manchester United players. pic.twitter.com/Pa4PqIoRbh.

It has been revealed that but so passive was their football that is the way he felt in the moment. For a club with United’s “attack, attack, attack” tradition – becoming something of a distant memory as seasons pass – that is a damning as it gets.

Neville’s Sky paymasters will be delighted by his emotive, insulting, headline-grabbing language. But he of course exaggerated a point to make a point. United, and Carrick, were, indeed, far too passive, lacking aggression, urgency and belief. They just do not press. United did, for too long, play like a team of dummies.

Against Fulham they almost played walking football until they conceded, desperation kicked in and they chased the game to salvage a late draw.

In a recent development, it begs the question: what is Carrick doing with this team? Yes, he may have been let down by no defensive signings in the summer – even if he must have bought into the strategy to prioritise a midfield rebuild – but he is far from absolved from blame.He will cling to the response to Lisandro Martínez’s own goal, to striking a post twice in the first half from Matheus Cunha and Bruno Fernandes, to managing to avoid a third successive defeat in a week, which would have led to the crisis klaxon being sounded. Carrick can talk about how ridiculous it would be to question his position as head coach. But is it?

It has been revealed that we now go into a three-week international break and the Premier League vacuum would have been filled by a debate over Carrick’s future, whether he is up to the job and another existential examination as to where United are heading. And who is to blame.

It has been revealed that that still might happen. United did not lose. But they were not remotely good enough, as has been the case for most of the season. Their only league win in five was against newly promoted Ipswich Town, having lost to newly promoted Hull City. They have also drawn at Everton and now at Fulham, who started the day bottom of the table and remain winless. Apart from facing Manchester City, it has hardly been the most taxing of starts. Except they are down in 12th and have not played well at all.

Recent findings suggest that it is not just that. Last year, United revamped their attack. Benjamin Sesko was absent through injury but are Cunha – despite his goal – Bryan Mbeumo and Marcus Rashford actually showing they are good enough? They, too, are passive and do not effect the play. Do not have that killer instinct. There is then an over-reliance on Fernandes. And if he does not do it, then who steps up?

In a recent development, that 15 minutes after half-time that culminated in the Martínez mishap was certainly woeful. But despite going close, United were also second best in the opening period, with Fulham’s 19-year-old academy product Josh King showing why he was so close to a senior England call-up. The forward ran riot, tormenting left-back Luke Shaw and was only denied by Senne Lammens. On more than one occasion, especially with a smart save with his right boot.

In a recent development, the goalkeeper was at the centre of Fulham’s goal, which was a shambles that summed up the state of United, who are just too easy to play against. And, so, Fulham’s captain Calvin Bassey was too strong for Cunha, who threw himself to the ground, looking for a foul, losing the ball from Kobbie Mainoo’s easy pass. The defender strode forward before Lammens parried his low shot, which then bounced off Martínez and back past the goalkeeper and into the net.

In a recent development, it was a Hammersmith End House of Horrors for United. To cap it all, Martínez then tried to blame Lammens who had, frankly, kept United in the game up until that point and could legitimately have told him where to go. And asked why he could not trap a ball and clear.

Fulham will certainly feel their own frustration. But with their fresh head coach Álvaro Arbeloa and an evolving team – if only striker Gonzalo García was more deadly – there are clear signs of optimism, having also just drawn at Liverpool.

Recent findings suggest that united’s late equaliser was fortunate. Yes, they applied pressure but to no real effect until Cunha’s shot deflected off the boot of Fulham defender David Affengruber as he tried to block, to wrong-foot goalkeeper Bernd Leno, who had also been outstanding. Recent findings suggest that but, once again, it was not up to the standard needed. And, like his team, be far less passive. Otherwise, he will not last.

In a recent development, might these games offer less possession and more counter-attacking chances? That’s glass half full.

In a recent development, I was purely referring to the fact that they walked around the pitch. I’ve never seen a Manchester United team walk around on the pitch that much.

Both teams were the same, I called them mannequins. I’ve never seen United walk around so much out of possession, no alertness, no being on your toes.

I wish he could play those attacking players, but they are going to kill him defensively.

Neither team appears too interested in gambling on the high press, a degree of wariness in their approaches. That was a nice Fulham move, sweeping from right to left, but Iwobi chipped a cross into Lammens’s gloves. Tielemans then looks for the run of Rashford with a through ball, but the forward is offside. Plenty of green grass behind Fulham’s back four though.

Recent findings suggest that fulham move the ball well again, Robinson setting the ball back for Garcia to strike from just outside the box but he dragged his shot wide of the near post. Too much time and space for the forward if you are United inclined, though. Tielemans then passes the ball out of play, splitting the difference between Dalot and Mbeumo.

Promising signs for Josh King as he carries the ball from the right touchline into a dangerous central position, unchallenged by United’s midfield. The home team have monopolised the ball so far, United sitting off in a shape, perhaps waiting for an error and the chance to counter-attack.

United get the game under way at Craven Cottage.

Recent findings suggest that very difficult to predict what you are going to be served by either of these teams. Both of their seasons are on a knife edge even at the this early juncture.

If Manchester United could choose a Premier League away fixture to revitalise their season, Fulham would be it. Not just because they are bottom of the league with just one point, albeit impressively earned last week away to Liverpool, but because United have not been beaten at Craven Cottage since December 2009 – although, not such a good omen for United, is the fact that Michael Carrick was in their team that day (playing at centre-back).

Michael Carrick dismissed as “ridiculous” any suggestion that his job as Manchester United’s head coach was at risk this early in the season. But he needs a positive result today against Fulham otherwise much of the prolonged international break will be taken up by debate as to whether he is up to it. United do not play again after today until they host stricken Tottenham Hotspur on October 10 and their start to this season has simply not been good enough. The concern for Carrick appears his inability to positively affect games when things are going against United.

Fulham starting XI: Leno, Castagne, Affengruber, Bassey, Robinson, Berge, Charles, King, Bobb, Iwobi, Garcia.

Sources indicate that the script pretty much writes itself these days. A flicker of optimism and hope of a fresh start giving way to the same old frustrations, complaints and inquests, the cumulative toll of which places an ever greater strain on a club mired in mediocrity but with little reprieve from the expectations that come with bearing such an illustrious name.

Michael Carrick states Pro Ref’s apology over the derby fiasco means little to Manchester United – but warned his players they cannot allow such setbacks to derail their season.

Chief refereeing officer Howard Webb formally apologised to United after the VAR officials Matt Donohue and Blake Antrobus failed to spot Enzo Fernandez was offside before wrongly allowing Erling Haaland’s winning goal to stand in Manchester City’s 1-0 victory at Old Trafford.

United were left shocked by the scale of the blunder, which came with 30 minutes of the game remaining and City already down to 10 men.

But Carrick has told his players not to become preoccupied with such injustices as they bid to overcome their poor start to the season before a crucial trip to Craven Cottage.

“It can have an impact in the moment of time, it can have a big impact, but we can’t let it have an impact on the rest of the season,” the United manager remarked.

Industry observers note that “That’s for us to get back to winning ways as soon as possible. Listen, one-off things can happen, at the time it was a pretty significant one, we know that. I don’t think I need to go over that.

“But yeah, I’ve got faith in it [VAR], it’s the system that we work towards and that we use so the apology doesn’t mean an awful lot.”.

Carrick added: “I can appreciate and I respect it for them putting their hands up and saying we got that wrong, I think it happens - it does happen.

Industry observers note that “But moving forward, yeah, we just have to deal with it, what’s thrown in front of us. And maybe we get one or two decisions on the back of how it balances out - percentages or law of averages or whatever that may be.

“But that was a pretty substantial one to take and had a huge impact on that game and that’s why it was particularly tough.”.

Michael Carrick may have had a point when he said it was “ridiculous” to question his future this early in the season, but this afternoon’s game at Fulham will shape the mood at Manchester United for the next three weeks.

A tally of four points from their first four games of the season is a disappointing start, and Brighton added to the sense of gloom in the League Cup by becoming the first side in 50 years to win from 2-0 down at Old Trafford.

With Champions League football on the agenda, that competition was at the bottom of United’s priority list but the ragged nature of the performance prompted boos around the stadium.

The no-show at Hull and defeat to 10-man City also fall into the “it’s how you lose” category of defeat, while there are widening fissures between the fanbase and the club’s hierarchy over ticketing policy and Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s political interventions.

The mood has also been sour at Fulham in the first few weeks of the season. In fact, they start the game bottom of the Premier League with one point, but do have the incentive of knowing a draw would take them above Spurs.

Following reports of friction between some established players and new head coach Alvaro Arbeloa though, they produced their best performance of the season in a goalless draw at Anfield last week when they had chances to win the game.

It has been revealed that fulham made nine changes in the League Cup in mid-week, but still ran out 3-2 winners at West Ham. Despite the west London club being an established mid-table Premier League team for a number of seasons, and United’s vulnerable state for the past few years, Fulham have beaten their opponent’s just once in the league since December 2009.Full team news on the way shortly.

#61009. Inside the 'uncomfortable' world of football documentaries: The shocking 'lack of respect' shown to managers, how Pep Guardiola learned to love the cameras - and why Mauricio Pochettino's appointment is bad news for Amazon's crew at Carrington

Inside the 'uncomfortable' world of football documentaries: The shocking 'lack of respect' shown to managers, how Pep Guardiola learned to love the cameras - and why Mauricio Pochettino's appointment is bad news for Amazon's crew at Carrington

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2104 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JACK GAUGHAN and NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER.
  • Published: 21:00 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 18 November 2026.
  • Paul Scholes and Phil Neville took charge of the Salford City team for one afternoon only, celebrity juxtaposed with the surroundings of a Northern Premier League Division One North fixture in a bracing January cold, played out before a few hundred supporters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JACK GAUGHAN and NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 21:00 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 18 November 2026.

Paul Scholes and Phil Neville took charge of the Salford City team for one afternoon only, celebrity juxtaposed with the surroundings of a Northern Premier League Division One North fixture in a bracing January cold, played out before a few hundred supporters.

It has been revealed that the club’s fresh managers, a double act from nearby Ramsbottom United, stood behind the goal studying the Salford squad. Neville approached them at full time, asking if they’d like to say a few words inside the dressing room – or more accurately, portacabin – by way of introduction.

‘It was dark at full time,’ co-manager Anthony Johnson recalls. ‘I’m not exaggerating the point, I opened the door and there were these cameras, these lights on. Nobody told us about a documentary.

According to recent reports, 'The lights literally came on and I went, “S***, I’m under the spotlight here”. There was no training, nobody sits you down to tell you how it works.’.

First airing in a primetime slot on BBC One, Salford’s Class of ’92 docuseries was hooked on the Manchester United legends owning the club but quickly became a show about the shouty personalities of Johnson and his partner, Bernard Morley, charting three promotions through non-League from 2015.

Industry observers note that salford are the smallest club ever to be the focus of this form of storytelling. Now, such documentaries are a popular vehicle for the country's elite.

Co-managers Anthony Johnson (left) and Bernard Morley became the accidental stars of a BBC documentary about the Class of 92's ownership of Salford City.

The celebrity of (from left) Paul Scholes, Nicky Butt, Ryan Giggs and Phil Neville was juxtaposed with Salford's humble facilities on the series.

The Amazon cameras were in for Manchester City’s title-winning campaign in 2018 and also collaborated with the club to document the end of Pep Guardiola’s reign.

Industry observers note that they are across town this year, right in the middle of United’s worst start to a season since the 1980s. Amid the infighting, public rows, Michael Carrick’s sacking and Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment, the streaming service should emerge as the real victors of what has been an inconceivably dismal three months at Old Trafford.

The sight of a camera crew scuttling out of a press conference with Carrick weeks before he was relieved of his duties, boom mic hovering, painted a neat picture of the additional stress that can be placed upon managers when the pound signs prove too large for executives to ignore.

‘You can’t be yourself,’ indicates Simon Grayson, Sunderland manager at the start of their infamous Netflix drama Sunderland 'Til I Die, with part one culminating in relegation from the Championship in the 2017-18 season. ‘You never forgot the cameras are there.’.

Like Johnson, Grayson had been unaware of the planned documentary. David Moyes rejected the idea the year before when he was Sunderland boss, just as Ruben Amorim did at United in 2025.

Industry observers note that grayson didn’t grant Netflix access to ‘the inner sanctum’ and provided them footage of training remotely. Wrexham boss Phil Parkinson has had the power to dictate where and when crews can film across their 57 episodes of Welcome to Wrexham.

It has been revealed that ‘I’m a private person,’ Grayson adds. ‘I don’t like people seeing what I’m doing. There were times when they actually tried to overstep the mark... you’d limit them to where the cameras would be.

'Even the players would say they were apprehensive and felt it was a bit intrusive. Aiden McGeady stated that he felt really uncomfortable doing it, as the rest of the dressing room did.’.

Vincent Kompany didn't like the way he was portrayed as a hot-head in a documentary during his time at Burnley.

Pep Guardiola relaxed his attitude towards the film-makers covering Man City when they learned where to position themselves in his dressing room without acting as a distraction.

Intriguingly, Guardiola embraced the cameras – but only eventually, initially insisting that filming could not resemble a circus. There was a scarcity of dressing room footage in Amazon’s 2018 edition. Only the notorious tirade at his players during half-time of a tempestuous FA Cup defeat at Wigan made it but that changed when City embedded their own production staff.

Sources say a relaxing of rules took time, around 12 months, as camera operators learned where to stand without acting as a distraction or finding themselves physically in the way.

City have been part of five documentaries in six years now, with Guardiola so enamoured by the producers that they became part of the backroom staff – even acting as auxiliary kit men on away days. He sent personal audio messages of thanks when he bid farewell last May.

He utilised them to create montages for pre-match speeches and leant on them to film players in slow motion to watch the gait of a player recovering from injury. That comes from the cameras being part of the furniture.

Critics will argue an in-house production is to the detriment of the eventual sanitised product, although City will point to Guardiola’s emotional breakdowns in A Beautiful Obsession – the story of his final season at City – as being raw and uncut.

The format is now moving towards in-season docs (regular episodes being available during a season rather than the whole show coming out at the end). This mirrors success stories in NFL and A Beautiful Obsession co-director John De Caux believes full-season pieces are ‘slightly on the wane’.

‘There were changes (in camera staff) all the time,’ Johnson states, reflecting on Salford’s annual series while he was in charge. ‘We were losing at half-time in one game… I make no apologies for this but I came in and went, “Move out of the f***ing way”. In previous seasons, they’d know not to be in that position.

Sources indicate that ‘You're having the same conversations again. It was like, "Hang on a minute. I've had this conversation before". The previous people knew about it. They have the footage from earlier seasons – so do your homework, like we all do with our jobs. It almost felt like a bit of a lack of respect at times.’.

The Spurs All or Nothing is memorable for an eye-popping scene between Danny Rose and Jose Mourinho, when the left back didn’t realise cameras were rolling.

Former Sunderland boss Simon Grayson was unaware of their planned Netflix documentary and didn't grant the producers access to his inner sanctum.

In a recent development, these are the challenges that Amazon face with United, somehow attempting to earn trust or forging relationships in a matter of months before they pack up and leave. The film crew will be seen as outsiders.

There is intrigue within the industry as to exactly how granular Amazon can go amid the United chaos and whether they use fly-on-the-wall cameras, as was the case with Arsenal (in 2021–22) and Tottenham (in 2019-20).

The Spurs All or Nothing is memorable for that eye-popping scene between Danny Rose and Jose Mourinho, when the left back didn’t realise the cameras were rolling.

Unlike Mourinho, Pochettino – his predecessor, sacked in November 2019 – had banned them from his office. He was never keen on the idea of the documentary and hardly features in the series, his dismissal coming early in Episode One – a sign perhaps that the film-makers got little out of him.

It will be fascinating to see if they gain access to his inner sanctum at United.

The club have had to double their media commitments this season as a result of the streaming deal, although they have been reluctant to organise sitdown interviews with players, telling Amazon that they must establish their own rapport for those.

Some clubs have been known to give their content away for free, with Sky Sports taking two seasons of Mission to Burnley without paying. The driving force behind those moves is to promote brands. Under Alan Pace’s premiership, Burnley are staring at potential relegation to League One.

Vincent Kompany, then the Burnley manager, is understood to have been vexed at his portrayal as a hot-headed screamer. Brendan Rodgers cannot have been overly pleased with Being: Liverpool, which ended in public ridicule and comparisons to David Brent. Players at other clubs have confided that they hid from cameras.

‘You can’t be yourself, you never forget the cameras are there,’ notes Grayson of his season alongside the makers of Sunderland 'Til I Die.

Salford's co-manager Anthony Johnson gives his players a dressing down in the BBC documentary.

Industry observers note that joey Barton, meanwhile, is still waiting for his moment – and may be for some time. Fleetwood Town commissioned their own team to chart his start in management and streaming giants Dazn purchased the rights.

Sources indicate that it was so close to being aired that Fleetwood held a premiere at Highbury Stadium for 100 supporters including the local mayor, only for one of Barton’s brushes with law enforcement in the intervening days to suspend the broadcast. Prolonged legal proceedings meant the idea was canned and Dazn’s licencing period expired.

It was later resurrected, focusing in part on then Fleetwood owner Andy Pilley’s fraud trial – a crew followed him into court on day one – but was then shelved when a guilty verdict was handed down. Cameras are following clubs up and down the EFL from Birmingham to Cambridge via Sheffield Wednesday.

Grayson, for his part, refused to share his drive home from training with the crew and now admits that the ultimately unfavourable edit may have been a result of him not giving the production firm what they wanted.

‘I did a presentation with the players with a flip chart and everybody thought it was an hour before kick-off of a league game,’ he says. ‘It was actually done at 11:30am before a pre-season game!

'That’s why I let them film it, because it was a pre-season game, and it had no real meaning. But they presented it in the doc as if it was before the first game of the season.

Recent findings suggest that 'Part of the severance when I was sacked was that I still needed to do some work for them. I did three different (choreographed) interviews in a London hotel with different shirts on after I’d been sacked, done as if they were filmed at the time.

Recent findings suggest that ‘People stated, “You didn’t come across that passionate about the club when you were talking about it”. Well, why would you when you were filming in November after you’d already been sacked? We were talking about deadline day in one of them. I’d already done something on that in August.

According to recent reports, ‘I think they had sympathy with me, but also if they’d had more sympathy, they wouldn’t have even asked me to do it. I’ve spoken to managers since and they’ve gone, “F***ing hell, you did well to put up with that".'.

Grayson only ever watched four episodes back and has heard his successor, Chris Coleman, was also dealt a raw deal.

Fabian Delph leads a Manchester City inquest during an FA Cup defeat at Wigan - the only scene from the dressing room that made it into Amazon's documentary on the 2017-18 season.

Mauricio Pochettino banned cameras from his office in his final days at Tottenham. Will he do the same at Manchester United?

By his own admission, Johnson enjoyed the process more than Grayson did. One ex-Salford player claimed that nothing was really cut from the show other than a fight on a team-bonding night out. It was authentic, no-holds barred.

Until the end of Johnson and Morley, that is.

According to recent reports, ‘We won the league and we ended up getting sacked anyway,’ Johnson notes. ‘We went to meet Gary (Neville) and the board. We went upstairs in Hotel Football and a cameraman followed us. Obviously they knew what was going on. When we got to the room for the meeting, they wouldn't let the camera in.

‘I'm actually smiling thinking about it. The documentary followed me and Bern everywhere, eating food or whatever, and then when the day comes to sack us, they didn't want the camera in the room!

‘The conversation was fine in the room itself but I think the perception from the outside world looking in would've been: "What the f*** is that all about?”’.

  • The 24-year-old joined Bayern in the summer of 2024 from Crystal Palace and has established himself as one of the finest wingers in European football.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Saikat Mandal | 20 Nov 2026 13:41, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 20:10.

Arsenal have reportedly joined Real Madrid in the race to sign Bayern Munich winger Michael Olise.

The 24-year-old joined Bayern in the summer of 2024 from Crystal Palace and has established himself as one of the finest wingers in European football.

The Frenchman has scored 54 goals and provided 61 assists in 122 appearances, although even those phenomenal numbers do not fully reflect what he brings to the Bayern side.

During the summer transfer window, Real Madrid were heavily linked with a move for Olise, but Bayern made it clear that the winger was not for sale at any price.

Bayern have reportedly placed a £265m valuation on Olise, who is under contract at the Allianz Arena until 2029.

However, club CEO Herbert Hainer has made it clear that no such asking price has been set for the player, whom they want to keep for many years to come.

According to Christian Falk, Arsenal are among the clubs interested in Olise, although it could prove difficult for the Gunners to prise him away from Bayern.

If Olise does decide to leave Munich, a move to La Liga could make more sense, having already experienced life in the Premier League.

There is also a significant gap between Olise's earnings and those of Harry Kane at Bayern, and the German club are expected to do everything in their power to convince the winger to sign a fresh contract.

In a recent development, the Bild journalist noted: "Every club has Michael Olise on their shortlist. There’s a lot of respect for Arsenal, but there are some really big players at the table, like Real Madrid.

"Olise has already played in the Premier League, so I strongly suspect a move to La Liga would be the next logical step were he to look for a move away from Munich.

Recent findings suggest that "That all remarked, Bayern Munich have proven that massive personal awards like the Ballon d’Or can still be won at FC Bayern. So, that’s the hope of the club and they’ll do everything in their power to keep Olise at the Allianz Arena.".

Olise could still be tempted to stay at Bayern after seeing his club teammate Harry Kane win the Ballon d'Or this year.

A move to a more competitive league could appeal to the Frenchman, while he may also want to join a club where his chances of winning the Champions League are high.

Bayern have not set an asking price for Olise and could demand a staggering fee, with paying such an amount likely to be nothing short of madness.

Arsenal arguably need a right winger who can provide reliable cover for Bukayo Saka rather than a player of Olise's calibre, who would expect to be a guaranteed starter if he made the move to the Emirates Stadium.

  • Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola has confirmed a quadruple injury boost for his side ahead of Sunday's blockbuster Premier League battle with Manchester United at Anfield.
  • The Reds have the honour of hosting Mauricio Pochettino's first game in charge of the Red Devils, in which they will endeavour to improve on a paltry record of just one win from five home matches in the 2026-27 top flight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 20 Nov 2026 14:06, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 14:06.

Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola has confirmed a quadruple injury boost for his side ahead of Sunday's blockbuster Premier League battle with Manchester United at Anfield.

The Reds have the honour of hosting Mauricio Pochettino's first game in charge of the Red Devils, in which they will endeavour to improve on a paltry record of just one win from five home matches in the 2026-27 top flight.

Liverpool maintained their excellent away form by beating Crystal Palace 3-1 before the international break, but Dominik Szoboszlai emerged as an injury worry following the Selhurst Park success.

The midfielder nevertheless joined up with Hungary for the November international break and played the full 90 in both of their Nations League games against Georgia and Northern Ireland, supplying two assists against the former.

Szoboszlai was managing a knee problem during his time with the Magyars, but speaking to the media on Friday, Iraola affirmed that the 26-year-old will be fine for Sunday's main event.

"He's in a good place, he's playing normally, he was not even strapped today so he's fine yes," Iraola responded when asked if Szoboszlai was still being carefully looked after.

As well as confirming Szoboszlai's availability, Iraola delivered positive updates on the Dutch trio of Ryan Gravenberch, Jeremie Frimpong and Virgil van Dijk.

The latter withdrew from the Netherlands squad for the November window due to an unspecified fitness problem, while Gravenberch and Frimpong were both absent from the win over Palace.

Frimpong sustained a hamstring injury against Brentford in October and has missed Liverpool's last six games in all competitions, while Gravenberch has been dealing with a minor heal fracture.

However, all three are in line to feature against old rivals Man United, as Iraola added: "If everything goes to strategy they should be available for the game.

"Gravenberch, it's a matter of pain, he's managing but he's been training the last two days. Jeremie is recovering the same. We've introduced him with the rest of the group, and Virgil is fine to go.".

Should all of Szoboszlai, Van Dijk, Gravenberch and Frimpong make the cut, Liverpool's only remaining concerns are the long-term trio of Conor Bradley, Giovanni Leoni and Hugo Ekitike.

The latter is still a while away from making a full recovery from an Achilles injury, but Leoni and Bradley have returned to team training as they close in on returns from serious knee injuries.

In a recent development, however, Iraola confirmed that neither defender will be in the squad on Sunday, adding: "The international break was the best moment to introduce them slowly, they've started doing things with the team. They are still not available, but it's very good news and I hope they can play in some weeks.".

Liverpool sit fourth in the Premier League table with 18 points from their opening 10 games, but they have won just two of their last nine matches against Man Utd.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER.

Published: 19:00 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 02:46 EST, 19 November 2026.

Mykhailo Mudryk has blamed his stint with the Ukrainian national team for the failed doping test which cost him two years of his career and revealed how fighting his case personally cost him millions of pounds.

The Chelsea winger, who is now on loan with Tottenham Hotspur, has opened up for the first time since he returned to football in the summer when his suspension was suddenly lifted.

It was in a two-hour interview with Ukrainian journalist Dmitry Gordon via his YouTube channel. While the title of the video mentions ‘suicidal thoughts’, Mudryk clarifies during the conversation that he did not consider committing suicide despite being in a dark place. ‘Kill myself – no, that’s not a way out,’ he said when asked that question.

But he did discuss how Chelsea broke the news of his failed test to him, whether they helped their £89million signing from Shakhtar Donetsk during his ban, his belief that the drug meldonium entered his system while he was in Ukraine, and why he is now with Tottenham. He further claimed that he has faced threats from gangsters, and admitted his dream is to someday win the Ballon d’Or.

On the Ukrainian national team and their federation, the Ukrainian Association of Football, Mudryk stated: ‘I’ll be honest, it pretended to help. But in reality, there was no help. They created more problems than they solved. Especially when we needed help the most, they turned their backs on us.

'I just would like, for the future, everyone to understand that you can only rely on yourself.'.

Mykhailo Mudryk has spoken publicly for the first time about the doping case that cost him two years of his career.

Mudryk has criticised the Ukrainian Association of Football over their support during his case.

Daily Mail Sport contacted the Ukrainian Association of Football for comment.

Industry observers note that continuing, Mudryk said: ‘The UAF is afraid of being left to blame in this situation, and afraid of the criticism or whatever else might come raining down. Distancing themselves from their own player, not helping, pretending to help, and in the end, first they drag the case out for months without really helping the case in the end. But at least the UAF isn’t to blame.’.

Mudryk was handed an initial four-year ban after being charged by the Football Association for failing a doping test, with his last appearance prior to that coming in November 2024 in the Conference League away at Heidenheim. He scored in that 2-0 win for Chelsea. He was able to return when a seismic resolution was struck after changes to the 'scientific reporting standards'. Mudryk appeared for Chelsea during their pre-season tour before joining Tottenham on loan.

Recent findings suggest that on how and why he failed his test, Mudryk stated: ‘I had never heard of a drug like meldonium, never seen it, never come across it in my life. I only learned about it when they told me the news. I definitely have ideas. It’s a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe.

Recent findings suggest that ‘This drug could only have got into my body where I was, and that’s Ukraine. There are no such drugs in England. It supposedly stimulates your heart and helps you, as far as I understand, handle physical load better.

‘I was at home and Chelsea’s management came to see me and they said we needed to talk. Then they say you’ve returned a positive doping test and now you’re facing a ban.

‘You can’t believe it’s true. You can’t believe this is happening to you. If I’d ever taken anything anywhere, I’d have understood that this conversation might happen one day.

Industry observers note that ‘At least I’d have understood it was possible. But when you spend a huge pile of money on watching your diet, on a nutritionist, on a chef. When you spend that much money every year on all these things, that’s the last thing you expect. Because it speaks for itself: that you take things very seriously, like nutrition, everything that goes into your body, you watch it very closely.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Otherwise there’d be no need to spend money on it, because you could manage without it. They tell you this news, and you sit there, and you kind of listen to them but don’t hear them.

Mudryk returned to action when his ban was lifted in August, with the winger revealing Xabi Alonso told him to get game time and that he was 'counting on him'.

The Ukrainian joined Tottenham on loan but has seen injury restrict his involvement to date.

According to recent reports, ‘At some point you just go into a trance. It feels like you’re falling in a dream off a skyscraper. You’re flying down, you feel yourself flying down, and only in a dream do you wake up when you hit the ground, but in real life you don’t wake up, you just keep falling. It hits you very hard mentally. At that moment the tears came later.’.

According to recent reports, mudryk revealed how ‘the figure is in the millions’ when asked about the lawyers fees which were needed to fight his case. He confirmed he paid for that himself, along with the personal trainers and massage therapists he used to maintain his fitness while suspended. However, Mudryk did add that Chelsea continued to pay his salary during his time out of football.

Sources indicate that on joining Tottenham and being reunited with Roberto De Zerbi, who formerly managed him at Shakhtar Donetsk, Mudryk stated: ‘It’s a perfectly logical decision. The club (Chelsea) has a new coach (Xabi Alonso), he sees football his own way. He sees the players he needs for that football. He came up and told me straight to my face: “You’d better go and play, get some game time, and then come back to Chelsea. I’m counting on you.”’ On De Zerbi, he added: ‘We met and he states: “Are you happy? Come on, we’ve still got a lot of work to do together.”’.

Mudryk added how difficult it was after switching to England and, along with encountering issues with his former representatives who encouraged him to move to Chelsea rather than Arsenal, he remarked: 'They give you ultimatums, you know. That’s how it is.’.

By Darren Plant | 20 Nov 2026 14:08.

Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has revealed that Joao Pedro remains unavailable for Saturday's Premier League fixture against Leeds United.

However, despite suggesting that he was dealing with fitness complications while on international duty with Ecuador, Moises Caicedo has been declared fit.

The Blues return to action this weekend sitting in fifth place in the Premier League table, yet Alonso is under pressure to deliver after four defeats in 10 top-flight matches.

Pedro has been sidelined since the October 17 game at Everton with a thigh injury, and it remains unclear when he will return.

Speaking at a press conference on Friday, Alonso stated that two players had been passed fit, while three players in total are still ruled out.

When quizzed on Pedro, the Spaniard told reporters: "Not yet. He's not fit yet to train with the team.

According to recent reports, "He's not going to be available for Leeds. We need to see game by game how he's feeling.".

Alonso went on to say that Maxence Lacroix, who suffered a hamstring injury versus Liverpool on October 28, was in a similar situation to Pedro, while Jorrel Hato remains out with a back problem.

Nevertheless, as well as Caicedo being passed fit, Josh Acheampong will be back in the squad after missing one Premier League game and two England Under-21 matches with a minor concern.

Meanwhile, Alonso has added that Reece James is still "some weeks away" from returning from a knee injury that required surgery.

However, despite not being back in contention this week, Alonso revealed that Jamie Gittens is training with the first-team squad after six weeks out with an ankle injury.

#61002. Global patterns and drivers of bee richness and endemism on islands

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 72m • 📚 Deep Dive (14471 w)

Global patterns and drivers of bee richness and endemism on islands

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 72 min read (14471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~72 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that islands account for a disproportionate share of global biodiversity1, yet insects, including invaluable pollinators such as bees2, remain underrepresented in island biogeography research3.
  • Islands are fundamental for studying patterns of biodiversity in time and space1,7.
  • Recent findings suggest that insects, the most diverse of all animal groups, remain underrepresented in global biogeographic studies and conservation assessments3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that islands account for a disproportionate share of global biodiversity1, yet insects, including invaluable pollinators such as bees2, remain underrepresented in island biogeography research3. Here we present a global checklist of island bees, recording 4,147 species across 305 islands. Although islands comprise only about 6% of the Earth’s land area, they support around 20% of known global bee diversity, and 42% of insular species are endemic, making up around 8% of all known bee species. Island bee species richness peaks at mid-latitudes (at least in the Northern Hemisphere), mirroring continental trends4. Native richness increases with island area and declines with isolation, consistent with patterns in other taxa5. The strength of island species–area relationships varies among biomes and is steepest in Mediterranean-type systems, which also support disproportionately high bee richness relative to flowering plant diversity. The number of endemic species is highest on large tropical islands, reflecting extensive in situ diversification. Major centres of bee endemism include Madagascar, Malesia (the Greater Sundas and New Guinea) and the Hawaiian islands, where a single large radiation of Hylaeus (Nesoprosopis) dominates6. Among islands that are capable of supporting endemic species, endemism scales strongly with total richness. These findings highlight the need to integrate island bee diversity into global conservation planning and position bees as a model for understanding insect evolution and conservation on islands.

Islands are fundamental for studying patterns of biodiversity in time and space1,7. The isolation and limited opportunities for colonization of remote islands have fostered evolutionarily distinct and highly endemic flora and fauna5,8,9. Consequently, islands have long been central to fundamental questions in macroecology, evolution, community ecology and species conservation10. Yet, despite their ecological and evolutionary importance, major gaps remain in our understanding of island colonization, evolution and diversification across animal taxa, especially arthropods.

Recent findings suggest that insects, the most diverse of all animal groups, remain underrepresented in global biogeographic studies and conservation assessments3. This gap largely reflects logistical and taxonomic challenges of assembling standardized, high-resolution data for insects across geographically and politically fragmented islands, which results in inadequate understanding of species’ distributions11. Consequently, tests of island biogeography theory have disproportionately focused on vertebrates (especially birds) and land vascular plants, and systematic studies across multiple archipelagos remain scarce both for insects and other invertebrates12,13,14 (but see Proios et al.15 for land snails).

Notable global efforts targeting other insect groups do exist, such as the Global Ant Biodiversity Informatics (GABI) database16, as well as efforts motivated by pest and pathogen spread, such as a global checklist of mosquito distributions17, and of patterns of island invasion by beetles18. Comparable progress has been made for Lepidoptera at regional scales, including recent large-scale analyses of butterfly biogeography across tropical Asian islands19. Nevertheless, comprehensive global syntheses—such as those available for plants20—of insect diversity and endemism across island systems are virtually absent.

It has been revealed that there are approximately 21,000 described species of bees worldwide21. They have an notable role in global ecosystems, pollinating many wild flowering plants22 and crops23. On continents, bees exhibit a bimodal latitudinal diversity distribution, with peak richness in seasonally xeric mid-latitude regions that support ecosystems with a Mediterranean climate (hereafter referred to as Mediterranean-type ecosystems), as well as in adjacent desert and montane habitats2,4,24. This pattern deviates from the latitudinal diversity gradients of most other groups of plants and animals, which usually peak in the tropics25. Although the continental-scale biogeographical and ecological patterns of bees are becoming better understood, how they translate to island systems remains underexplored.

In a recent development, generalizations about island bee biogeography have hitherto been rather qualitative in nature. For example, Michener2 noted that whereas very small bees might be carried over long distances by winds, wood-nesting bees may have dispersed across oceans via driftwood: a rafting hypothesis supported by quantitative evidence that wood-nesting bees are overrepresented in island faunas26, Michener also suggested Polynesian transport by seafarers for certain wood-nesting bee taxa that reached some of the most remote oceanic archipelagos, such as the Hawaiian islands. Consequently, bees detected by the even the first European voyages of discovery cannot be assumed to be native.

In a recent development, recent phylogenetic evidence indicates that several bee lineages colonized fresh biogeographic regions during the Neogene Period (around 23–2.6 million years ago) via island-hopping, showing how stepping-stone dispersal may have shaped bee composition. For example, the families Apidae, Megachilidae and Halictidae probably colonized Australia via movements from mainland Asia across the Indomalayan Archipelago27. Similar processes have been proposed to explain disjunct distributions in modern day Central America, where ancient archipelago chains acted as stepping stones between North and South America before the continents joined2.

According to recent reports, conversely, disjunct distribution patterns in other bee groups appear to reflect their more limited capacity to disperse and subsequently colonize islands. For example, following the breakup of Gondwana, stingless bees (Apidae, tribe Meliponini) appear to have been unable to cross the substantial marine barriers that appeared, and their present distribution in Indomalaya probably reflects episodes of sea level fluctuation and transient land-bridges, rather than long-distance overwater dispersal28.

These examples indicate the importance of accurately documenting insular bee diversity to achieve a more complete and fine-grained understanding of global bee biogeography and conservation. Yet, despite this need, comprehensive data remain sparse. Only 542 bee species have been assessed for the global International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, including just 240 species recorded from islands and 68 island endemics. Of these assessed species, 26 are considered threatened, and for many of these, distributional data are not publicly accessible29. The limited representation of island taxa on global conservation lists does not reflect the well-established vulnerability of island biotas: for example, the majority of US federally listed endangered bee species are native Hawaiian endemics30.

Here we present a global assessment of native bee diversity on islands. Specifically, we investigate: (1) global patterns of native bee richness and endemism; (2) the influence of island characteristics (area and isolation), topography (elevation) and climate variables on both native bee richness and endemism; (3) how endemism scales with richness; and (4) the relationship between insular bee diversity and angiosperm richness. We expect the patterns of insular bee richness and endemism to be shaped by area and isolation, as predicted by island biogeography theory7, but also by biotic and climate constraints and associations, including mutualistic relationships with flowering plants22.

By addressing these questions, our analyses fill knowledge gaps, providing a global baseline for investigating the evolutionary and biogeographic history, ecology and vulnerability of island bees, while highlighting priority regions for future research and conservation at both archipelago and single-island scales. More broadly, this baseline enables rigorous tests of major hypotheses in island biogeography and (meta)community assembly1 using this taxonomically diverse, and ecologically and economically key group.

Our final dataset consists of 11,065 unique island-native bee species combinations, representing 4,128 native species across 305 islands (see Methods for details of this classification) (Fig. 1a). Consequently, of the approximately 21,000 bee species described worldwide, our data indicate that 20% occur on islands. Of these, 42% (1,742 species) are restricted exclusively to islands, accounting for around 8% of all described bee species. Although this proportion is lower than that reported for vascular plants, for which 21% of the global flora are island endemic, with 14.5% single-island endemic species (SIEs)9, as well as terrestrial mammals (about 12% single-island endemics31) and rodents specifically (about 17% endemics to islands32), it nevertheless represents a slightly higher contribution of islands to global bee diversity relative to the approximately 5–6% of global landmass represented by islands globally1. Although we focus here on native bee richness, we also recorded introduced species to distinguish genuine native diversity from non-native species accumulation. We identified at least 54 species as introduced on 143 islands, with the western honey bee (Apis mellifera) being by far the most widespread, introduced to 127 islands in our dataset (Extended Data Table 1). Invasion due to anthropogenic drivers is a major threat to insular diversity33, and evidence, at least for A. mellifera, suggests negative effects of invasive bees on native biodiversity on islands (see, for example, ref. 34).

According to recent reports, a, Map of global bee diversity on islands (n = 305 islands). Each circle represents an island for which there are recorded native bee species. The colour gradient is log-scaled and indicates the total number of native bee species recorded for each island; the size of the point or circle is proportional to the total number of endemic species found on each island. Endemism is measured as the total number of island (or island group; Methods) endemic species. Left, histogram showing the total number of endemic bee species by latitude. Right, histogram showing the total number of bees on islands by latitude (5° latitude steps; native richness maximum = 3,552 species (35° to 40° N), endemism maximum = 298 species (−10° to −5° N). Note that this pattern does not control for variation in the number and size distribution of islands across latitude (but see Fig. 2). Islands marked with an X have recorded bee species consisting exclusively of non-native species. b, Upset plot showing global distribution of bee species endemic to and shared between islands in different zoogeographical realms62 and the mainland. Of 4,128 native bee species found on islands, 1,742 are recorded only from islands, representing an 8.4% share of global bee diversity that is unique to islands. Each bar highlights the number of species unique to that geographic combination. Coloured bars and coloured realm names represent the number of species endemic to islands within that realm. Coloured circles indicate island-only comparisons. Grey bars indicate species that are shared across the island realms or mainland. Island base map in a adapted from ref. 63.

Recent findings suggest that bee species richness peaks in the Western Palaearctic Realm, whereas endemism (species only found on islands within these realms) is highest on Indomalayan (466 species) and Australasian (443 species) islands (Fig. 1b). Clear differences in island bee richness are also apparent among biomes (Fig. 2), however this pattern is influenced by variation in island area. Species richness was highest in Mediterranean-type biomes: Sicily (approximately 25,000 km2, 636 species), is the island with the highest species richness worldwide and Cyprus (approximately 9,300 km2, 384 species) has the highest species richness of the oceanic islands. The East Aegean islands (approximately 5,000 km2, 589 species) also support large bee faunas, dominated by widespread continental species, reflecting their limited degree of isolation. In contrast to the high richness, endemism on these islands is low, with only Crete (14 species) and Cyprus (23 species) showing comparatively high levels of island endemism. Despite its proximity to the Levant region and its complex origins in tectonic uplift, Cyprus is treated here as an oceanic island owing to its lack of historical land bridge connections to the mainland. The most species-rich Mediterranean-type oceanic island of strictly volcanic origin is Tenerife (2,000 km2, 57 species).

a, Biome-specific ISARs. Solid lines represent fitted mean regression lines from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Slopes (β) are reported for each biome. Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island. Labelled islands are the top 10% most species-rich islands within each biome; values in parentheses show total native bee richness. b, Relationship between island isolation (log10 distance to mainland) and native bee species richness. The effect of isolation was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = −0.13, 95% confidence interval [−0.21, −0.04], t(208.0) = −2.96, P = 0.003). The solid line represents the fitted mean regression line from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Point colour indicates the proportion of SIEs. c, Predicted bee species richness by island type (continental, fragment or oceanic) from the full mixed-effects model, holding other predictors constant (predictions represent an island of median area (around 445 km2), median isolation (approximately 605 km from mainland) and median sampling coverage (35% after sample-size adjustment, raw median 79%). Circles and lines indicate the model-predicted mean ± 95% confidence intervals, with the number of islands shown below each category.

According to recent reports, tropical islands, by contrast, account for moderate overall native species richness compared with Mediterranean-type islands but markedly higher levels of endemism. Upcoming Guinea supports 284 species, of which 210 (73%) are endemic, making it by far the richest island in the Australasian realm. The nearby Maluku Islands archipelago (34,000 km2) hosts 102 species, including 62 endemics (61%), and includes Seram (18,000 km2), the most species-rich tropical, oceanic island for bees (87 species).

In the Neotropics, Hispaniola represents the most species-rich oceanic island, with 66 species. In the Nearctic, the predominantly oceanic California Channel Islands (approximately 910 km2) have a high overall richness (154 species) but low levels of endemism (5%). In the Afrotropics, Madagascar stands out with 226 species, of which 201 (89%) are endemic. Within Oceania, which consists only of oceanic islands, the Hawaiian islands (17,000 km2) are a major hotspot, with all 65 native species of wild bees belonging to a single lineage of Hylaeus (Nesoprosopis), and endemic to the archipelago6. Among other oceanic systems, the Mediterranean-climate Canary Islands (approximately 5,400 km2) host a similarly high number of endemic species (57 out of 128 species), although at a lower proportional level of archipelago endemism (AE) (45%).

Globally, bee richness on islands peaks in the Northern Hemisphere at mid-latitudes (Fig. 1a), mirroring the mid-latitude peak of bee richness observed on mainlands4. This pattern contrasts with the latitudinal diversity gradient seen in other diverse insect groups, such as ants, whose global richness peaks predominantly in the tropics35. The lack of an island-specific bimodal diversity pattern comparable to that found for the mainlands2,4 is probably a consequence of the limited number of Mediterranean-type islands in the Southern Hemisphere. This asymmetry reflects the true distribution of islands globally36, and not simply sampling bias; our global dataset confirms data availability and sufficient coverage across these regions (Fig. 3). This pattern occurs both on continental and oceanic islands, although many of the larger islands within the Mediterranean-type biome were continental or complex in origin. Such environments favour diverse wild bee assemblages through a combination of evolutionary history and ecological conditions. Bees are thought to have originated in the arid environments of Western Gondwana2,27, with limited but predictable rainfall that generates short yet intense blooming periods and a high flowering plant diversity in open habitats2,4,37. These conditions promote temporal synchrony between bee flight periods and floral resources, fostering increased specialization and resource partitioning that reduces competition. This synchrony promotes local speciation and therefore increases richness, allowing these regions to defy the traditional latitudinal diversity gradient2. Our global results support these conclusions but trait-based research focusing on the biome-specific patterns of habitat and dietary specialization of bees on islands are needed to directly test these claims.

Map shows the geographic distribution of bee sampling effort and completeness across islands worldwide. Circle size represents the average number of individual records (specimens or observations; see Methods, ‘Island bee occurrences and global checklist’) collected per species on each island, with larger circles indicating greater sampling effort. Circle colour indicates sampling completeness measured as the sample-size-adjusted sample coverage (ranging from 0% (yellow) to 100% (purple)). The index combines Chao–Jost sample coverage64 with a weighted-by-sampling effort, based on the total number of occurrence records. Islands with dark purple colouring and large point sizes represent well-sampled regions with high confidence in richness estimates. Yellow and orange points represent under-sampled islands where true diversity is likely to be underestimated. Coverage was calculated using a species/island abundance (count of all occurrences per species per island) matrix of all records to estimate the proportion of the total individuals per island that belong to the observed species, using a non-parametric estimator that accounts for the frequency of rare species (singletons and doubletons). Because coverage can vary by sample size (for example, appearing high when based on very few records), we also applied a sample-size adjustment that scales coverage by the total number of occurrence records. n = 303 islands. Island base map adapted from ref. 63.

According to recent reports, to test fundamental aspects of MacArthur and Wilson’s theory of island biogeography7 for bee diversity, we used a mixed-effects model with archipelago identity as the random effect. The final best model was selected based on Akaike information criterion corrected for sample sizes (AICc) and included log10-transformed island area in km2 and its interaction with biome, as well as isolation (log10-transformed distance to continental mainland in km) as fixed effects. This model explains 66% of the variance in species richness through fixed effects (area, isolation, island type and biome), and 75% variance when including archipelago identity (conditional R2). This moderate difference in R2 values indicates that native richness is strongly governed by broad biogeographic variables, with some unexplained regional structure.

Island area highlights a consistent positive effect on native bee richness but the island species–area relationship (ISAR) slopes differ significantly among biomes (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Table 1). Mediterranean-type biomes showed the strongest species–area response (β = 0.50), which is significantly steeper than that of all other biomes (Supplementary Table 2). Tropical islands exhibit an intermediate effect, (β = 0.28), which is indistinguishable from temperate islands (β = 0.18). By contrast, desert (β = 0.02) and boreal (β = 0.02) islands display flatter slopes, indicating that island size is not a major constraint on bee diversity in these biomes. The impact of biome on species area slopes is observed more clearly on oceanic islands (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 3), specifically, the ISAR slope for Mediterranean-type islands is significantly greater than for the others. This is not the case for continental islands, where these ISAR slope differences are far less pronounced (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 3).

Richness decreases with island isolation (β = −0.13, P < 0.003) (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 1), corresponding to a reduction of roughly 15% in species richness for each tenfold increase in distance from the mainland. This isolation effect is uniform across all biomes, supporting the fundamental principle that remote islands receive fewer colonists and consequently maintain lower richness as a function of their area7. We also observe a clear influence of island type on richness. Oceanic islands support substantially fewer species than continental (β = −0.19, P = 0.01) and fragment islands (β = −0.27, P = 0.01; Supplementary Table 2), consistent with their lack of past land connections to the mainland, more limited historical species pools and generally younger geological ages, whereas a high proportion of continental shelf islands were connected to the mainland only a few thousand years ago, leading to more ‘harmonic’ biotas1. Alternative models (ΔAICc < 2) additionally include positive relationships with temperature seasonality and annual precipitation. Neither climate variable has a statistically significant effect (Supplementary Table 4).

Our results support the conclusion that ISARs can vary considerably as a function of island geo-environmental properties12,38. Specifically, bees may benefit from biome-specific increases in ecological complexity in Mediterranean-type biomes owing to temporal differences in habitat availability, which can permit increased richness even at small scales, resulting in area having a stronger effect on richness than in tropical or temperate biomes2,4. The finding that Mediterranean-type islands in our models have the steepest ISAR slopes and highest richness values align with the high seasonality of the climate and flowering plant diversity characteristic of Mediterranean climates39, providing diverse nesting sites and floral resources throughout the year.

Recent findings suggest that although biomes explain considerable variation in richness on islands, they represent broad proxies for climate and habitat diversity. The steep ISAR slope for Mediterranean-type systems suggests that explicitly measuring finer-scale variables, such as resource availability and microhabitat diversity, may provide deeper insights into the mechanisms underlying island bee biogeography. Habitat diversity and environmental heterogeneity, and the potentially associated diversity of mutualist partners, can constitute important predictors of species richness40. In our global models, these factors are likely to be implicitly incorporated when comparing between islands by combining area and biome. However, a single biome classification masks within-island variation as for many large islands with a high elevational range, such as Madagascar, Tenerife, New Guinea or Hawai’i (Major Island), representing the island as a single biome inevitably underestimates its pronounced environmental heterogeneity, which is recognized as a driver of high species diversity and endemism40. Additionally, regional geographic context is an important consideration, as shown by the islands of Lesvos and Cyprus, which show comparatively high species richness values for their area (positive residuals from the Mediterranean-type ISAR; top 5% among Mediterranean-type islands). These islands sit at the border between the European bee fauna and the exceptionally rich western Asian fauna, and the resulting high comparative species richness for their area may be due to this dual species pool from which bees can colonize41.

Sampling effort is uneven across regions, as expected for a global dataset (Fig. 3), with parts of Oceania, Indomalaya and Australasia being comparatively under-sampled. To account for this heterogeneity, we included sampling completeness, measured as the proportion of individuals belonging to observed species and weighted by sample size, as a fixed effect in the native richness model (Supplementary Table 1). Completeness has a positive effect on native bee richness (β = 0.21, P < 0.001; Extended Data Fig. 3). Islands with a greater sampling completeness tend to have higher estimated richness. However, controlling for sampling completeness does not weaken the central results above. The island–biome–area effects remained strong after adjusting for sampling completeness confirming that these patterns were not a result of uneven sampling effort. This indicates that the relationships between area, isolation and richness, and in particular the contrast between mid-latitude richness and high tropical endemism, reflects true ecological differences (Fig. 3). Future efforts to digitize and provide open access to museum collections42,43, conduct targeted expeditions to historically difficult-to-sample islands2,44 and harness citizen science platforms such as iNaturalist45 will be critical to resolving knowledge gaps in island bee diversity, an important task given the projected gaps in global bee diversity46.

According to recent reports, to identify the biogeographic and climatic predictors of endemism and assess whether richness can explain endemism patterns, we tested the same linear mixed-effects models as for native richness (Fig. 4a,b). Across islands capable of supporting SIEs (SIE ≥ 1, n = 113), area is associated with increased SIE richness (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 5) and this relationship varies significantly with biome, as observed for richness. However, unlike richness, biome-specific area slopes for SIE differs significantly between tropical and temperate islands, with a steeper relationship in tropical islands (Δ = 0.27, P = 0.01), whereas the difference between tropical and Mediterranean-type islands was marginal (Δ = 0.28, P = 0.06; Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 6). Isolation (log10-transformed distance to nearest landmass larger than 1,000 km2) has only a weak, non-significant positive influence (β = 0.09, P = 0.11; Fig. 4a,b). Temperature seasonality had a significant positive effect on SIE (β = 0.28, P = 0.018), and sampling completeness and elevation range each appeared as significant positive predictors in alternative models within ΔAICc < 2 (Supplementary Table 7). We note that sampling completeness could bias endemism estimates in both directions, overestimating endemism on well-studied islands where the same species have not yet been recorded elsewhere, and underestimating it where undiscovered endemics remain.

In a recent development, the observed patterns are consistent across data subsets but without the interaction of area and biome. On oceanic islands with endemics (n = 69), area remains the strongest predictor (β = 0.32, P < 0.001, R2 = 0.38; Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 5). Among islands rich in SIE (>5% of native richness; n = 96), SIE richness increases with area (β = 0.36, P < 0.001, R2 = 0.66) and increases marginally with sampling completeness (β = 0.16, P = 0.02) (Extended Data Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 5). These results parallel global patterns of vascular plant endemism on islands47. The mid-latitudinal peak in bee species richness2, seen on islands predominantly in the Northern Hemisphere, does not translate into increased bee endemism. Rather, bee endemism is greatest in the tropics (Extended Data Fig. 5). Patterns for AE are broadly similar. Across islands hosting AEs (n = 217) area was again the main predictor and interacted with biome (Supplementary Table 5). However, AE–area slopes were consistent across tropical, temperate, and Mediterranean-type biomes, with only desert islands showing a significantly lower rate than tropical islands (Δ = 0.35, P = 0.01; Supplementary Table 6). Isolation (distance from mainland) is non-significant (β = −0.04, P = 0.48) and sampling completeness is also included as a significant effect, suggesting that islands with high numbers of AEs are also the best studied (β = 0.14, P = 0.01). Additionally, there is a significant positive effect of elevation (β = 0.18, P = 0.01) suggesting that topographically complex islands support a greater diversity of endemics at the archipelago scale (Extended Data Fig. 6).

A model predicting SIE from overall native richness alone shows a clear correlation (R2 = 0.44) and improved significantly with the inclusion of biome (ΔR2 = 0.15, χ2 = 33.1, P < 0.001; Supplementary Table 8). Although adding the interaction term yields a significant model improvement (ΔR2 = 0.02, χ2 = 8.15, P = 0.04), post hoc pairwise comparisons reveal no significant differences in slopes between biomes after correcting for multiple testing (Supplementary Table 8). This indicates a practically uniform global rate of increasing SIE with richness but with distinct baseline shifts; specifically, Mediterranean-type islands support significantly fewer baseline SIEs than all other biomes (Extended Data Fig. 7). Conversely, for AEs (R2 = 0.55), the full interaction model results in the best fit (ΔR2 = 0.14, χ2 = 72.54, P < 0.001; Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Table 8), demonstrating that the rate endemic species accumulate with increasing richness is biome-dependent. Pairwise comparisons indicate that the slope for Mediterranean-type biomes (0.42 ± 0.10) is significantly flatter than in desert (0.83 ± 0.12, P = 0.02), tropical (0.96 ± 0.03, P < 0.001) and temperate (0.75 ± 0.06, P = 0.01) biomes, indicating a partial decoupling between richness and AE (Supplementary Table 9). Although Mediterranean-type islands generally support fewer AEs than expected across the richness gradient, the Canary Islands stand out as an exception, showing high AE richness consistent with their high overall richness, although probably enhanced by their relative isolation from the primary Mediterranean source pool (Extended Data Fig. 6). This divergence also highlights that the AE model probably captures more ancient diversification compared with the SIE model48,49. This partial decoupling contrasts with vascular plants, for which the richest islands also tend to host the highest numbers of endemic species, particularly in the case of large tropical islands9. Our results are consistent with previous macroecological studies50, suggesting that the relationship between richness and endemism is not simple and varies among taxa.

Together, these findings reveal that bee endemism is concentrated on large tropical islands and certain oceanic archipelagos rather than in areas of peak species richness globally. New Guinea and Madagascar stand out for supporting both high numbers and high proportions of endemic species. By contrast, certain other island systems, including the Caribbean, the Philippines and the Hawaiian islands, are characterized by only a high proportion of endemics. This apparent divergence between patterns of richness and endemism suggests a distinction between the factors structuring island assembly attributable to colonization and evolutionary diversification in bees. Wet, humid tropical conditions, combined with greater isolation of many oceanic tropical islands, present environmental barriers to bee colonization2. Therefore, successful colonizers are presented with greater ecological opportunity, and this can lead to high in situ diversification1. These patterns suggest distinct evolutionary histories: high endemism in Madagascar probably reflects multiple independent radiations51, whereas in other systems single radiations account for high proportions of endemism, such as Palaeorhiza in New Guinea52, Hylaeus (Nesoprosopis) in the Hawaiian archipelago6 and Lasioglossum (Homalictus) across Pacific islands such as Samoa and Fiji53,54. Conversely, the factors that support high richness in Mediterranean-type islands are likely to include: (1) the adaptation to arid environments; but also (2) frequent arrivals from nearby continental source pools, providing sufficient gene flow to inhibit in situ diversification and thus result in lower endemism55. Globally, bees provide evidence that endemism, and by extension extinction risk, is not inextricably linked to overall species richness, often diverging into regions of high endemism but low richness or high richness with low endemism56.

Building on these findings, we additionally examine how plant diversity, as a potential biotic driver, covaries with bee richness, given that bees depend strongly on flowering plants for food and nesting resources22,24. Across the 175 islands for which we have both angiosperm richness data and native bee richness, we observe a positive correlation: angiosperm richness alone explains 49% of variation in bee richness across islands (R2 = 0.49), a relationship that persists after accounting for island area and isolation (β = 0.64, P < 0.001; Fig. 5a and Supplementary Table 10). The slope of the relationship between angiosperm and bee richness is largely consistent across biomes (likelihood ratio test: χ2 = 7.02, P = 0.06). However, temperate islands show a slightly steeper relationship compared with the tropical baseline (β = 0.55, P = 0.015; Fig. 5a and Supplementary Table 10). Additionally, we observe differences from the baseline in total supported bee richness in Mediterranean-type islands: they support 5.6 times more bee species than tropical islands at equivalent plant richness, area and isolation (P < 0.001; Fig. 5b and Supplementary Table 11).
