The faunal assemblages from the Baxian and Naxian caves are taxonomically diverse and remarkably similar in composition (Supplementary Information 3 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Both assemblages include numerous taxa that have since become locally extinct, including Pongo, Elephas and rhinoceros Dicerorhinus, though most remain extant elsewhere in Asia. Notably, H. erectus, Stegodon and ‘Megalovis’ are globally extinct. Habitat preference analysis indicates that both assemblages are strongly dominated by forest-dwelling taxa (Supplementary Fig. 3), which is consistent with predominantly forested landscapes during the time of deposition.

The plant-equivalent stable carbon isotope values for the Baxian faunal teeth, after correction for species-specific diet-to-enamel enrichment factors based on body mass29 (Supplementary Information 9), range from −31.5 to −23.0‰ (average = −27.6 ± 1.87‰ (1σ)), while lower values observed at the Naxian cave range from −34.0 to −25.1‰ (average = −29.4 ± 2.45‰ (1σ)). Both assemblages yield values well below the dense-canopy forest threshold of −27.5‰ (ref. 28), with no evidence of C4 plant consumption or even C3–C4 intermediate signatures (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 9). These data indicate that the fauna at both sites derived their dietary carbon exclusively from C3 vegetation, with the frequency of canopy-related values exceeding those reported for equatorial African rainforest systems29 and being comparable to that documented for western Amazonian forests30,31,32. This pattern is particularly notable given that several of the taxa represented in the assemblages are known elsewhere to exploit mixed C3–C4 resources or to incorporate substantial C4-derived inputs into their diets in more open environments16.

Independent oxygen isotope (δ18O) and clumped isotope (Δ47) analyses further support these environmental reconstructions, indicating humid tropical conditions with higher precipitation and cooler temperatures than modern values in this region (Extended Data Fig. 9 and Supplementary Information 9 and 10).

Sources indicate that three H. erectus teeth from the Naxian cave (NX-B1, NX-B2 and NX-A1) show similarly low isotopic values, with carbon values ranging from −15.0 to −14.0‰, which fall at the boundary between dense-canopy forest and more open C3 vegetation. Although the dataset is limited (n = 3) and presently restricted to the Naxian locality, these values are fully consistent with those observed across the much larger faunal assemblage and fall within the range expected for consumers deriving their dietary carbon from closed-canopy C3 vegetation, demonstrating that these late H. erectus populations exploited tropical rainforest resources.

It has been revealed that high-resolution trace element mapping on one H. erectus individual from the Baxian cave (PA1799) yielded 87Sr/86Sr ratios ranging from 0.7110 to 0.7220 (Supplementary Information 11 and Extended Data Fig. 10), while three H. erectus teeth sampled from the Naxian cave showed overlapping but distinct ranges. All four individuals indicate either movement between geologically distinct regions or consumption of resources from multiple locations during childhood (2–6 years), corresponding to the period of tooth formation.

Sources indicate that A regional strontium isoscape for southern China and northern Southeast Asia33 (Supplementary Information 11) reveals substantial spatial heterogeneity in predicted 87Sr/86Sr ratios, with the local Baxian–Naxian region characterized by relatively homogeneous values (0.710–0.715), reflecting the dominant Carboniferous–Permian limestone karst geology (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 10). More radiogenic signatures (0.717–0.723) occur to the west and northwest in mountainous areas underlain by Precambrian and Palaeozoic metamorphic rocks, while intermediate to more radiogenic values (0.715–0.720) characterize regions to the south, including the Red River valley of northern Vietnam.

Geographic assignment probability maps generated for three representative 87Sr/86Sr values observed in the human tooth profiles indicate that these H. erectus individuals may have moved between the local limestone karst regions and more distant areas during childhood, with the most radiogenic signatures potentially pointing towards areas as far afield as northern Vietnam, which connect southern China with mainland Southeast Asia (Figs. 1 and 3 and Extended Data Fig. 10).

Industry observers note that our results demonstrate that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 8), representing, to our knowledge, the youngest reliably dated occurrence of this species in China and the first with robust chronological constraints from southern China. The integration of multiple independent dating techniques combined with Bayesian age modelling provides unprecedented temporal resolution for late H. erectus in mainland Asia. These findings fundamentally alter our understanding of the species’ persistence and distribution in China, extending the documented record by more than 200,000 years beyond the previous youngest occurrences in Hexian and Nanjing14,15, and establishing southern China as a key region for late-surviving populations during the late Middle Pleistocene (for example, ref. 19).

The temporal importance of this discovery extends beyond simply filling a chronological gap. The age uncertainty range of 324–184 ka places these H. erectus populations at some point within marine isotope stages 9 through 6, raising intriguing questions about potential contemporaneity or overlap with Homo longi (Denisovans) identified in Cobra cave (Laos)34, Baishiya cave (Tibetan Plateau)35, Harbin (northeast China)36,37,38 and the Penghu Channel off the western shore of Taiwan39. The temporal proximity of these various hominin populations across China during the late Middle Pleistocene suggests a more complex biogeographical landscape than previously recognized, with multiple hominin lineages potentially coexisting across different ecological zones and elevational gradients.

Moreover, the environmental context revealed by our multi-proxy analyses challenges prevailing assumptions about late H. erectus ecological constraints and mobility patterns. The combined evidence demonstrates unequivocally that these late H. erectus populations exploited closed-canopy tropical rainforest environments and may have conducted long-distance movement beyond the local karst terrain during childhood. The ecological implications of this rainforest use and mobility are profound. Archaeological evidence has so far suggested that H. sapiens was the only member of our genus to specialize in the regular exploitation of these environments18, as early as 150 ka in western Africa40,41. In Southeast Asia, recent isotopic observations of declines in C4 environments and expansion of rainforest in the Middle to early Late Pleistocene have been associated with the disappearance of non-H. sapiens hominin taxa42,43, seemingly unable to shift from mixed savannah–woodland habitats to these increasingly closed forests16,44. However, our data directly challenge this view by demonstrating that H. erectus was not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments (Fig. 3) and that long-distance mobility into these environments may have been a common behavioural pattern rather than exceptional behaviour by isolated individuals.

These findings contrast markedly with Early and Middle Pleistocene H. erectus occupations at Trinil3 and Sangiran in Java4 (Extended Data Fig. 9b). The youngest Javanese H. erectus at Ngandong2 persisted in relatively open woodland refugia2, leading to suggestions that expanding rainforests may have contributed to the species’ eventual extinction in Java2,16. Among early hominin-bearing sites in East and Southeast Asia (Extended Data Fig. 9b), the Naxian and Baxian cave results most closely resemble those from Lida Ajer, Sumatra (73–63 ka), an early H. sapiens site also characterized by closed-canopy rainforest45. This demonstrates that H. erectus was, at minimum, capable of persisting among rainforest fauna, even if such habitats did not represent its optimal ecological niche.

In a recent development, areas in northern Vietnam, such as the Red River valley (Figs. 1 and 3), have long been recognized as a critical biogeographical corridor connecting the karst uplands of southern China with the lowlands of mainland Southeast Asia24. The limited strontium isotope evidence tentatively suggests that late H. erectus populations may have been utilizing similar corridors for seasonal movements, long-distance migrations or resource procurement. This large range (potentially around 250 km) through mostly enclosed environments challenges assumptions about the limited ranging behaviour of H. erectus and suggests behavioural sophistication in landscape use.

Our findings collectively demonstrate that late Middle Pleistocene H. erectus was present in southern China, surviving contemporaneously with H. longi and exhibiting considerable ecological and behavioural flexibility. Rather than being restricted to open savanna or woodland habitats, as traditionally assumed, these populations persisted in closed-canopy tropical rainforests while simultaneously engaging in potential long-distance mobility across diverse ecological and geological landscapes. This evidence challenges the characterization of H. erectus as a species unable to exploit complex tropical forest environments. Whether these adaptations were specific to the late-surviving populations in southern China alone remains to be seen, but further stable isotope work on other Middle Pleistocene sites is vital to address this question. However, the presence of morphologically and genetically confirmed H. erectus in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, combined with the environmental and suggested mobility evidence, is sufficient to necessitate a re-evaluation of the species’ adaptive capabilities, biogeographical range and ultimate fate in mainland Asia.

It has been revealed that the caves were discovered using local knowledge and targeted reconnaissance hunting for breccia in the rear chambers. The locations of test pits within the caves were selected on the basis of these reconnaissance surveys. Excavation grids were based on the shape of cave passages and distribution of fossil-rich deposits. Jackhammers were used to break blocks of fossil breccia, and the fossils were extracted using geological hammers. Fine cleaning, identification and cataloguing were conducted in the laboratories at Shandong University and the Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Palaeoanthropology (IVPP).

The fossil-bearing breccia and associated sediments from the fossil chambers of both caves were sampled in situ under subdued red-light conditions (Fig. 2a,d) and were processed using standard sample purification procedures for quartz and feldspar separation including a 40% and 10% wash in hydrofluoric acid for 45 and 10 mins, respectively46. Single aliquots of 90–125 µm feldspar and 180–212 µm quartz or feldspar grains were processed in a Riso TL-DA-20 equipped with an automated DASH set-up, a dual-laser single-grain attachment47 and a blue- and ultraviolet-sensitive Electron Tube photo-multiplier tube (PDM9107Q-AP-TTL-03), using either a blue filter pack (Schott BG-39, 2 mm, and Corning 7-59, 4 mm) for feldspars or U340 filters (2 × Hoya U340, 3.5 mm) for quartz. Data were collected using Sequence Pro v.4.65 and analysed in Analyst v.4.57, DRAC v.1.3 and on spreadsheets designed in Microsoft Excel 365 v.2607. Feldspar equivalent doses were corrected according to the results of the anomalous fading tests (using a weighted mean fading rate of 2.0 ± 0.2% per decade)48, but no residual corrections were undertaken, and the equivalent doses for both feldspar and quartz were then run through either a central age model for the single-aliquot results or a minimum age model49 to identify the single-grain population that experienced the most bleaching before burial. All luminescence analysis was conducted at the ‘Traps’ luminescence dating facility at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia.

Industry observers note that measurements of 238U, 235U, 232Th and 40K were estimated using Geiger–Muller multi-counter beta counting and thick-source alpha counting of dried and powdered sediment samples in the laboratory, combined with in situ gamma spectrometry in the field. The corresponding (dry) beta and gamma dose rates were obtained using the conversion factors in ref. 50 and the beta-dose attenuation factors in ref. 51. Cosmic-ray dose rates were estimated from previously published relationships52, making allowance for the sediment overburden at the sample locality (ranging from 3.99 to 0.20 m), the altitude (ranging from 2,000 to 176 m above sea level) and geomagnetic latitude and longitude of the sampling sites.

Seven H. erectus teeth from the Naxian (n = 6) and Baxian (n = 1) caves were analysed for U-series dating across two laboratories in China and Australia. U-series measurements were undertaken using a laser-ablation multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (MC-ICP-MS) at the Geoarchaeology and Archaeometry Research Group (GARG), Southern Cross University, according to protocols in ref. 53 and in a Neptune MC-ICP-MS at the School of Geography Science, Nanjing Normal University according to refs. 54,55. Laser ablation (at Southern Cross University) was performed with a New Wave Research 213 nm laser, and thorium (230Th, 232Th) and uranium (234U, 235U, 238U) isotopes were measured on a Thermo Neptune XT MC-ICP-MS. Teeth were ablated using rasters of 5 min each and were measured with standards before and after. Uranium and thorium were separated using conventional anion-exchange chromatography at Nanjing, and the U–Th solution was then introduced into the MC-ICP-MS via a DSN-100 desolvation nebulizer system. Isotopic ratios were measured using a detector configuration that allows for the simultaneous measurement of U and Th isotopes56,57.

One H. erectus tooth and one Pongo tooth from the Baxian cave (n = 2) were selected for coupled ESR and U-series dating at GARG, Southern Cross University. Enamel fragments from each tooth were separated using a hand-held diamond saw following the protocol developed in ref. 58. Fragments were then measured at room temperature on a Freiberg MS5000 ESR X-band spectrometer at a modulation amplitude of 0.1 mT, 10 scans, 2 mW power, 100 G sweep and 100 kHz modulation frequency. Each fragment was irradiated, following exponentially increasing irradiation times. Sediment elemental concentrations, external beta and gamma dose rate contributions, and water content were obtained from in situ measurements. The external beta-dose rates have been extrapolated from the U, Th and K contents measured on a portion of sediment sub-sample (approximately 8 g). The external gamma dose rates were determined in situ using a portable gamma spectrometer at each site. The equivalent doses were estimated using Matlab-based MCdose software v.2.0.

In a recent development, separate sub-samples were hand-drilled from the fresh cross-section of the in situ capping flowstones from Naxian and Baxian caves and processed at the Radiogenic Isotope Facility, University of Queensland (n = 6), and six soda straws and one sample of secondary calcite cement were processed at the School of Geography Science, Nanjing Normal University (n = 7). The powdered sub-samples were subjected to chemical treatment and isotopic measurements by mass spectrometry56. U-series dating of the speleothem samples were conducted at the University of Queensland using a Nu Plasma MC-ICP-MS, and analytical procedures followed previous publications for MC-ICP-MS57,58,59. The 230Th/234U ages were calculated using Isoplot EX 3.75 (ref. 60) and half-lives of 75,690 years for 230Th and 245,250 years for 234U (ref. 61). U-series dating of the speleothem samples was carried out at Nanjing Normal University using a Neptune MC-ICP-MS. U-series ages were calculated using the half-lives of 75,584 years for 230Th and 245,620 years for 234U (ref. 62). Non-radiogenic 230Th was corrected using an assumed bulk-Earth atomic 230Th/232Th ratio of (4.4 ± 2.2) × 10−6 (refs. 54,55).

Two Bayesian modelling programs were used to analyse selected independent age estimates (n = 43) (Supplementary Information 8) and to evaluate the uncertainties associated with the combined dating techniques applied to both sites (Supplementary Tables 7–15): OxCal (v.4.4.4, available at https://c14.arch.ox.ac.uk/oxcal.html)63 and ChronoModel (v.3.2.7, https://chronomodel.com/)64. The analyses incorporated the probability distributions of individual ages, constraints imposed by stratigraphic relationships and the reported minimum or maximum nature of some of the individual age estimates. Each individual age was included as a Gaussian distribution (with mean and s.d. defined by the age estimate and their associated uncertainties), and the resulting age ranges for each phase of deposition were presented at 2σ. OxCal allows the identification of boundary ages between each layer to constrain the fossil layer and ChronoModel was applied to assess the extent to which identical or similar data could be obtained. Both modelling results have been presented for transparency.

Three H. erectus specimens from the Naxian cave, as well as 47 faunal teeth from the Baxian cave and 38 from the Naxian cave (n = 41 in total), were taxonomically identified and prepared for stable isotope analysis, following established preparation methods65 (but see refs. 66,67). The resulting δ13C and δ18O values were measured using a ThermoFisher MAT253+ in six separate measurement blocks per sample at the Earth and Environmental Sciences’ Stable Isotope Geochemistry Laboratory at the University of Queensland. The evolved CO2 gases from the Naxian teeth were analysed for carbon and oxygen isotope compositions using a Thermo Delta V Advantage isotope ratio mass spectrometer housed at the Key Laboratory of Archaeological Sciences and Technology, Shandong University. Stable isotope measurements on the three H. erectus teeth were carried out at the Service de spectrométrie de masse isotopique du Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle, Paris, and analysed using a Thermo Delta V Advantage isotope ratio mass spectrometer. To assess isotopic differences among sites, we applied non-parametric and multivariate tests. For univariate comparisons, Kruskal–Wallis tests revealed highly significant differences in both δ13Ccarbon source (χ² = 181.5, d.f. = 6, P < 0.001) and δ18O (χ² = 114.4, d.f. = 6, P < 0.001) among sites. All statistical analyses were conducted using the open-source program R software (v.4.5.1)68.

Three in situ samples were collected in bulk (CBAX2, CBAX3, CBAX4) from the breccia at Baxian and the clumped isotope analysis was undertaken in the Macquarie GeoAnalytical Stable Isotope Facility using a ThermoFisher dual-inlet MAT253+ mass spectrometer. The results were processed using the Easotope software package69. The final Δ47 value for each sample was then averaged and reported with 95% confidence intervals, before temperatures were calculated using the calibration in ref. 70 for 90 °C reactions. Using these temperatures, the oxygen isotopic composition of the precipitating fluid (δ18Ofluid) was calculated using the equation in ref. 71.

It has been revealed that one H. erectus tooth from Baxian was sectioned with a high-precision diamond saw and polished to a smoothness of greater than 5 μm. Laser ablation combined with ICP-MS was used for trace elemental mapping analyses using an ESI NWR193 coupled to an Agilent 7900 ICP-MS at GARG, Southern Cross University, according to the procedures in refs. 19,72. A laser spot size of 40 μm, a scan speed of 80 μm s−¹, a laser intensity of 60% (approximately 1 J mm−2) and a total integration time of 0.50 s were used to produce data points that corresponded to a pixel size of approximately 40 × 40 μm. NIST610 and NIST612 (certified standard reference materials) were used to assess signal drift. Strontium isotope analysis (87Sr/86Sr) was conducted on four H. erectus teeth: one from Baxian cave and three from Naxian cave, also using laser-ablation MC-ICP-MS at the GARG facility. Enamel fragments were carefully extracted from regions showing low uranium concentrations and distinct elemental signatures from the surrounding dentine according to the mapping results. To contextualize the 87Sr/86Sr values obtained and assess potential mobility patterns, a regional strontium isoscape was constructed for southern China and northern Southeast Asia. The isoscape modelling was based on random forest ensemble machine learning analyses adapted from the original script developed in ref. 33 and followed the method fully described in ref. 21.

All isoscapes generated using random forest machine learning were based on the global bioavailable strontium database in ref. 33 and all R scripts necessary for generating isoscapes are available at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21131183)74.

K.E.W., Y.Z., R.J.-B., W.L., W.W., C.J., Y.W., W.Y., Y.P. and L.Y. explored and excavated the sites and collected faunal and dating samples, K.E.W. conducted the luminescence dating, R.J.-B., W.Y. and Q.S. conducted the U-series and coupled U-series–ESR dating of the teeth, and J.-x.Z. and Q.S. conducted the U-series measurements on the speleothem. R.J.-B. conducted the trace element analysis and V.B. conducted the isoscape work. M.Q., S.M., L.H. and A.-M.B. conducted stable isotope analysis on the fossil teeth, and N.B. and P.R. conducted isotope data analysis. M.Q. and S.M. conducted the clumped isotope analysis of the breccia, Y.Z., Y.P. and A.-M.B. analysed the fauna and K.E.W. designed the dating approach and conducted the Bayesian modelling. R.K., C.Z., W.L., R.D.Á., F.W., Z.W. and Q.F. worked on the hominin teeth. Finally, K.E.W., R.J.-B., W.L. and Y.Z. wrote the paper, with contributions from all co-authors.

According to recent reports, a-d Naxian cave, a and b the cave – location marked with a red star - is situated on the outer cone of a karst inselberg located close to a highway. c a montage of images to demonstrate the speleology of the cave with the small entrance and flowstone step that leads into the stalagmite chamber dense with speleothem, a larger chamber with narrow and high ceilings and terminating with a small fossil chamber with breccia, d the fossil bearing breccia at the highest point of the cave capped with flowstone and underlain by a younger underlying mixed material below. e-h Baxian Cave e and f the cave is also situated on the outer edge of a karst cone with the limestone corridor than connects both caves, cave location is marked with a red star, g a montage of images to demonstrate the speleology and sedimentology of the cave from the wide and high entrance to the narrower and smaller passage that lead to the confined fossil chamber, h the fossil bearing breccia at the highest point of the cave capped with flowstone and underlain with the younger underlying mixed material. There is a remarkable similarity between the stratigraphy and sedimentology of these deposits and associated fossils (d, h).

According to recent reports, a Naxian profile, b Baxian profile illustrating the changing speleology and cave deposits from the upper fossil chambers down to the entrances. Baxian is longer than Naxian but slopes at a lesser angle than the steeper Naxian. Images illustrate the main features found in both caves including a wider chamber and smaller fossil chambers. The images of the fossil chambers are taken from a 3D models of the caves (Supplementary Information 2 for links).

The enamel curve shows a broader temporal sensitivity, while dentine exhibits steeper p-value responses reflecting higher susceptibility to uranium migration. b: Normalised uranium-uptake curves for enamel (red) and dentine (green) showing contrasting U-uptake kinetics, with enamel characterised by delayed uptake and dentine by more rapid early incorporation. c: Frequency distribution of modelled ages generated under the US-ESR age model, illustrating the central tendency and dispersion of the Monte-Carlo age simulations used to derive the final age estimate, d H. erectus tooth from Baxian that was dated using US-ESR techniques (Supplementary Information 6).

Recent findings suggest that a and b are the dating results (n = 43) as separate age estimates in kyr for the five dating techniques modelled according to Oxcal and applied to the sediments and fossils of Naxian (a) and Baxian (b) caves. Data are presented as mean values +/− SD. The techniques are colour coded according to the legend and organised into the unit in which they were sampled from – the flowstone, breccia or underlying clay. Some of the techniques represent minimum ages (such as the US ages on teeth) and contain a colour coded arrow pointing the right, while other represent maximum ages such as the pIR-IRSL single aliquot dating of feldspars and contain a colour coded arrow pointing the left. The thick black horizontal boxes with dashed lines represent the boundary ages (and errors) estimated by the modelling. The boundary ages quoted represent the upper and lower age ranges for the breccia units in both caves. c and d are the dating results (n = 43) as separate age estimates in kyr modelling according to Chronomodel for the same five dating techniques. Data are presented as mean values +/− SD. The individual sample events have been organised into three phases; breccia deposition (including fossil and sediment ages), overlying flowstone precipitation and underlying clay deposition with each phase represented by a different plot. The timescale goes from more recent on the right (50 ka written as -50000) to oldest on the left (400 ka written as -400000). For Baxian (c) we have used the age uncertainty at 2 σ (95%) of the fossil teeth dated using US-ESR (H. erectus and Pongo), resulting in an age of 324-184 ka. For Naxian (d), the fossils are all dated using US only so represent minimum ages, so instead we have used the period between the overlying flowstone (as the minimum age) and the youngest soda straw in the breccia (as the maximum age) both at 2 σ (95%) uncertainty to constrain the age of breccia deposition at 319-241 ka. The use of Chronomodel compared to Oxcal has accentuated similar events and reduced the younger age uncertainty by around 20 kyr. The overlapping uncertainty between the two caves has been used to represent a Homo erectus presence at some point between 324-184 ka.

Recent findings suggest that a Taxon-specific δ13Ccarbon source values in relation to vegetation type. δ13Ccarbon source (plant-equivalent values; ‰ VPDB at Baxian (324-184) and Naxian (319-241 ka). Shaded background areas indicate ecological zones: dense canopy forest (dark green), C3 vegetation (light green), and C4 grassland (yellow). The unshaded interval between C3 and C4 represents the C3–C4 intermediate zone. This framework allows direct comparison of faunal isotopic signatures against expected vegetation regimes. A large proportion of taxa from both sites fall within the dense canopy forest zone, supporting the interpretation of closed-canopy rainforest environments. The H. erectus values (red stars) fall within the C3 forest domain and plot at the boundary between dense canopy forest and more open C3 vegetation. b Vegetation zone proportions at hominin-bearing sites in Southeast Asia and South China. Proportional distribution of faunal δ13Ccarbon source values assigned to vegetation zones (dense canopy C3, open C3, C3–C4 intermediate, and C4). Bars show the relative contributions of each zone across six hominin-bearing sites: Trinil4, Sangiran5, Cobra Cave34,73, Duoi U’Oi74, Lida Ajer45,75, Baxian and Naxian. Baxian and Naxian are dominated by C3 signals, with substantial contributions from dense canopy vegetation, while Trinil and Sangiran show higher proportions of intermediate and C4 values, reflecting more open habitats. Lida Ajer is strongly weighted toward dense canopy values, consistent with closed rainforest settings. Together, these results illustrate marked ecological contrasts between late H. erectus contexts in China and Javanese sites, as well as affinities between Naxian and the rainforest environment of early H. sapiens at Lida Ajer75,76,77.

In a recent development, a Trace element distribution maps of the Baxian H. erectus tooth. LA-ICP-MS elemental maps showing the distribution of (i) 7Li/43Ca, (ii) 88Sr/43Ca, (iii) 138Ba/43Ca, and (iv) 238U/43Ca ratios normalised to calcium across a longitudinal section of the tooth. All maps show both enamel (upper/left portion, blue-green colours) and dentine (lower/right portion, predominantly dark red). The colour scales are optimised to visualise variation within the enamel tissue. Dark red areas in the dentine for Sr, Ba, and U maps indicate significantly elevated concentrations due to post-depositional diagenetic uptake from the burial environment, rendering these tissues unsuitable for life history reconstruction. In contrast, the enamel tissue displays lower concentrations and visible banding patterns, particularly Ba/Ca, and Sr/Ca maps, which reflect biogenic signals. The U/Ca map clearly illustrates the extent of diagenetic alteration, with the highest concentrations in dentine and at the enamel-dentine junction (EDJ), demonstrating the vulnerability of dental tissues to post-depositional elemental exchange. The Li/Ca map highlights elevated concentrations in both tissues with distinct banding in the enamel. All measurements were obtained using LA-ICP-MS with 40 μm spot size and Ca-normalization to account for matrix effects. b Strontium isotope ratio profiles across H. erectus tooth enamel from Baxian and Naxian caves. LA-MC-ICP-MS 87Sr/86Sr ratio profiles measured along linear transects across tooth enamel from (i) BAX-1 from Baxian Cave, and (ii) NX-A1, (iii) NX-B1, and (iv) NX-B2 from Naxian Cave. The x-axis represents distance in mm along the ablation transect from the cervical region toward the cusp, corresponding to the temporal sequence of enamel formation from early to late childhood. The y-axis shows 87Sr/86Sr ratios, with variation reflecting changes in geological substrate accessed through diet and drinking water during tooth formation. All four individuals exhibit substantial intra-tooth variation in 87Sr/86Sr ratios that exceeds analytical uncertainty, indicating mobility between geologically distinct regions or consumption of resources from multiple locations during childhood. BAX-1 shows 87Sr/86Sr ratios ranging from 0.7110 to 0.7220, while the Naxian specimens display overlapping ranges: NX-A1 (0.7115-0.7165), NX-B1 (0.7095-0.7165), and NX-B2 (0.7100-0.7160). The observed variation patterns provide evidence for landscape mobility of late Middle Pleistocene H. erectus populations in southern China. c Strontium isoscape and geographic assignment probabilities for H. erectus mobility in southern China and northern Southeast Asia. (i) Regional-scale strontium isoscape showing predicted bioavailable 87Sr/86Sr ratios across southern China, northern Vietnam, northern Laos, and adjacent regions. Colours indicate 87Sr/86Sr values ranging from 0.710 (dark blue) to 0.725 (pink), with the Baxian/Naxian cave sites marked by a white dot. Major cities (Hanoi, Lào Cai, Guilin) are shown for geographic reference. (ii) Prediction uncertainty map for the regional isoscape, showing standard error of predicted 87Sr/86Sr values ranging from 0.004 (yellow, low uncertainty) to 0.016 (purple, high uncertainty). (iii) Local-scale isoscape focused on a 400 km × 400 km region centred on the Baxian/Naxian sites, with scale bar representing 50 km. (iv) Prediction uncertainty map for the local isoscape (v-vii) Geographic assignment probability maps for three representative 87Sr/86Sr values observed in H. erectus tooth enamel: (v) Seq1 = 0.714, representing average values for NX-A1 and lower values in NX-B2, showing high assignment probabilities (yellow-green) concentrated within 30-50 km of the cave sites in limestone karst terrain; (vi) Seq2 = 0.719, representing transitional values observed in multiple specimens, showing assignment probabilities extending southward ~150-250 km toward the Red River valley region; (vii) Seq3 = 0.724, representing the most radiogenic values observed (particularly in BAX-1), showing assignment probabilities concentrated in the Red River valley foothills approximately 250 km south of the caves and near Lào Cai to the west, with very low probabilities in the local cave area (dark purple). The progressive southward shift in assignment probabilities from Seq1 to Seq3 indicates long-distance mobility of late H. erectus individuals between the local karst uplands and distant regions up to 250 km away during childhood tooth formation. All isoscapes generated using random forest machine learning based on33 global bioavailable strontium database.
